items.explanation_markdown:
You and a friend have tomorrow planned out: walk to the park, find a bench, eat the lunch you packed the night before. Then you look up. The sky is the colour of wet paper. Your friend wants to know what happens to the plan in that case, and you need a sentence that hangs the whole afternoon on something that has not happened yet.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|stem|降[ふ]っ}}たら、{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}に{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きません}}。
```

*If it rains tomorrow, we're not going to the park.*

Nothing has rained. Nothing has been cancelled. All you have done is build a fork in the road: one branch has rain on it, and on that branch there is no park. Setting up that fork is the entire job of たら.

## How it works

The recipe is short enough to feel like a trick. Take the plain past form of a word — the one ending in た — and stick ら on the end. That is the whole pattern.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}} → {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}たら
{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} → {{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}} → {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ん}}だら
```

*eat → ate → if/when (someone) eats*
*drink → drank → if/when (someone) drinks*

Look at the second one for a second. {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} does not become `飲みたら`; its past tense is {{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}, so the conditional — the form that means *supposing this happens* — is {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ん}}だら. Same story with {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}} → {{oyogu|ta|泳[およ]いだ}} → {{oyogu|stem|泳[およ]い}}だら. That is where the だら you sometimes see listed as a separate form comes from. It is not a second rule to memorise; it is the same ら glued onto a past form that already ended in だ. Get the past tense right and だら takes care of itself.

The irregulars stay boring, which is a genuine relief: {{suru||する}} → {{suru|ta|した}} → {{suru|stem|し}}たら, and {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} → {{kuru-v|ta|来[き]た}} → {{kuru-v|stem|来[き]}}たら. No surprises, no extra sounds.

There is a reason this pattern is built on the past form rather than the dictionary form, and it is worth two seconds of your attention. The た form in Japanese is not purely about yesterday — it marks an event as **completed**. たら takes that completed event and says *treat this as done, and now what?* Once you hear it that way, the fact that one pattern covers both *if* and *when* stops being strange. Both of them are just "this is finished — next".

### Adjectives and nouns join in

たら is not a verbs-only club. い-adjectives have a past tense of their own, so they take ら exactly the same way: {{yasui-adj||安[やす]い}} → {{yasui-adj|ta|安[やす]かった}} → {{yasui-adj|stem|安[やす]かっ}}たら.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}が{{yasui-adj|stem|安[やす]かっ}}たら、{{kau-v|masu|買[か]います}}。
```

*If this book is cheap, I'll buy it.*

な-adjectives and plain nouns lean on だった instead: {{hima||暇[ひま]}} → {{hima||暇[ひま]}}だった → {{hima||暇[ひま]}}だったら, and {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}} → {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}だった → {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}だったら. Nothing new to learn there either — if you can make the past tense of a noun sentence, you can make its conditional.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}{{hima||暇[ひま]}}だったら、{{issho-ni||一[いっ]緒[しょ]に}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}を{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ません}}か。
```

*If you're free tomorrow, shall we watch a movie together?*

Notice what the second half of that one is doing. It is not a prediction — it is an invitation. たら is perfectly comfortable with a request, an invitation, or a suggestion after the comma. The fork is allowed to end in *let's*, not only in *this will happen*. Hold onto that; it turns out to be one of the main things that separates たら from the other conditionals waiting for you.

Negatives need no new machinery, because every ない form behaves like an い-adjective: {{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からない}} → {{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からなかった}} → {{wakaru|stem|分[わ]から}}なかったら.

One ordering rule, and it does not bend: the たら clause comes first. The condition is the setup, the second half is the payoff, and Japanese will not let you deliver them in the other order.

### When "if" is really "when"

English forces you to choose between *if* and *when*, and the choice leaks information. *If I get home* sounds like there is some chance you won't. Japanese simply refuses to make you decide — たら covers both, and the listener works out which one you meant from how likely the first half is.

```jp
{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{kaeru-v|stem|帰[かえ]っ}}たら、{{sugu||すぐ}}{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}します。
```

*When I get home, I'll call you right away.*

Nobody hearing that thinks getting home is in doubt. The first event is a certainty, so たら reads as *once that's done* — a sequence, not a gamble. Same shape as the rain sentence, same grammar, and the only thing that changed is how sure everyone is about the first clause. This one trips people up in the first week, and the fix is not more grammar: it is noticing that Japanese is leaving something to context that English spells out.

### The past-tense version is a different animal

Put the second half into the past tense and たら stops predicting anything at all. Now it reports. You did the first thing, and the second thing was already sitting there waiting for you.

```jp
{{reizouko||冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]}}を{{akeru|stem|開[あ]け}}たら、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{iru-exist|masu|いました}}。
```

*When I opened the fridge, there was a cat.*

You opened a fridge and met a cat. That mixture — one small ordinary action, and then something nobody ordered — is exactly the flavour of past-tense たら. It is how Japanese says *and then, of all things...*, and it shows up constantly in stories about your own day.

## Rules and exceptions

- Build it from the past form, never the dictionary form. `行くら` and `飲みたら` are the two wrong guesses everyone makes, and both come from skipping the past-tense step in the middle.
- The たら half stays plain, always. Politeness is settled once, at the end of the sentence: {{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}します is polite, {{kaeru-v|stem|帰[かえ]っ}}たら is not, and the sentence as a whole is polite anyway.
- The たら clause goes first. There is no version of this where you tack the condition on at the end as an afterthought.

> When the second clause is in the past tense, whatever follows たら has to be something that happened *to* you — a discovery, a surprise, a result you did not steer. `冷蔵庫を開けたら、猫を買いました` breaks, because buying is a decision, and you cannot discover your own decision.

> たら is not a machine for translating every English *if*. If the *if* you have in mind is really the reason for something that already happened, you have reached for the wrong tool — that is ので territory, and the two of them are worth seeing side by side.

## Casual speech

たら has no contracted form to learn; it is already about as short as Japanese gets. What it does have is a casual habit — people cut the sentence off right after it and let their voice carry the rest.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{kiku-v|stem|聞[き]い}}たら？
```

*Why don't you ask the teacher?*

Rising intonation, and the missing second half is something like *wouldn't that sort it out*. It is a suggestion, not a question about the past, and every bit of its force lives in the pitch. Say it to a friend and it sounds helpful. Say it to your own boss and it lands somewhere between blunt and nagging, so keep this one for people at your level or below.

## たら against ので and のに

Here is the comparison that makes たら click. The form {{furu-rain|ta|降[ふ]った}} — the past of {{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}} — turns up in all three of these patterns. The only thing that changes is what you hang on the end of it.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|ta|降[ふ]った}}ので、{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}に{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きませんでした}}。
```

*Because it rained, we didn't go to the park.*

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|ta|降[ふ]った}}のに、{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}に{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きました}}。
```

*Even though it rained, we went to the park.*

Both of those are reports from the real world. ので says the rain happened and it was the reason we stayed in. のに says the rain happened and we went anyway, which was mildly ridiculous of us. Neither one leaves any doubt about the weather: it rained, full stop.

Now put the very first sentence of this lesson back next to them. The core is the same {{furu-rain|ta|降[ふ]った}}, but that little ら turns the rain from a fact into a possibility. Nothing has been settled, nobody has stayed home, and the sentence is describing a branch of the future rather than a piece of the past.

So the test is quick. Has it already happened? Then you want ので for the reason, or のに for the contradiction. Has it not happened yet — or has it not happened *so far as you know*? That is where たら lives.

One line to carry away: past form plus ら, and your sentence splits neatly into *this is done* → *then that*. Everything else is just noticing whether the first half is a gamble or a certainty, and trusting context to tell your listener which. Soon you will meet ば and なら, two more ways to say *if* — ば for what is always true, なら for *well, if we're talking about that* — and たら is the one that will carry your conversations comfortably while you sort those two out.
caution_notes: Build たら from the plain past form, not the dictionary form — if the past tense ends in だ, the conditional ends in だら.
Politeness is decided by the final verb only, so the たら clause itself stays plain even inside a polite sentence.
The たら clause always comes first; the condition is the setup and never an afterthought tacked onto the end.
With a past-tense second clause たら reports something you ran into, so it cannot be followed by an action you deliberately chose.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in a shop, staring at a price tag, trying to decide whether to buy something. You already know how to say {{takai-adj||高[たか]い}}です — it's expensive — but what you actually want is a personal rule, something that applies not just today but every time you're in this situation: expensive means no. That's the job of ば. It builds a general-truth "if," the kind that states a standing condition rather than describing one specific moment.

```jp
{{takai-adj|stem|高[たか]けれ}}ば、{{kau-v|masu|買[か]いません}}。
```

*If it's expensive, I won't buy it.*

Think of ば as the Japanese version of the "if X, then Y" you'd write in a rulebook or a recipe, not the "if" you'd use to describe one particular afternoon. Nobody's talking about this one item on this one day — the sentence is a policy you carry around with you, ready for the next price tag and the one after that.

It attaches to the end of whatever sets up the condition, and the shape it takes depends on what kind of word that is — a verb, an adjective, or a noun / な-adjective. Four families, four small changes. None of them are hard once you see the pattern underneath, and you already know every verb and adjective involved; this lesson is really just teaching you one new ending to bolt on.

That's also why ば is worth learning properly instead of skimming: it's the ending you reach for constantly once you start noticing how much of daily talk is really a string of small standing rules — what you do when it's late, what you buy when it's cheap, what happens when a friend calls. English handles all of that with one word, "if." Japanese wants you to first decide whether you're stating a rule or narrating an event, and only then pick the right ending.

## How it works

**Group 1 verbs** — the ones ending in う, く, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む, or a る that doesn't behave like an い/え-stem verb — shift their final sound from the u-row to the e-row, then add ば. {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} (to speak) becomes {{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]せ}}ば. This is the same row-shift you'll eventually recognize all over the language; here it's just doing conditional duty instead of something else.

```jp
{{yukkuri||ゆっくり}}{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]せ}}ば、{{wakaru|masu|分[わ]かります}}。
```

*If you speak slowly, I'll understand.*

**Group 2 verbs** — ones like {{miru-v||見[み]る}} or {{taberu||食[た]べる}} whose stem already ends in an い or え sound before る — just drop the る and add れば. The irregular {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} follows the same shape, which is one less thing to memorize separately.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}が{{kuru-v|stem|来[く]れ}}ば、{{ureshii||嬉[うれ]しい}}です。
```

*If he comes, I'll be happy.*

**{{suru||する}}**, the other irregular, becomes {{suru|stem|すれ}}ば. Every verb built on {{suru||する}} — {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}, {{renshuu-suru||練[れん]習[しゅう]する}}, and every other noun-plus-{{suru||する}} verb you've picked up — inherits this same change automatically, so you never have to look it up twice.

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]すれ}}ば、{{jouzu||上手[じょうず]}}に{{naru-become|masu|なります}}。
```

*If you practice every day, you'll get good at it.*

**い-adjectives** drop the final い and add ければ. The plain negative ない rides along on this same rule, since grammatically it behaves exactly like an い-adjective — it ends in い, so it conjugates like one.

```jp
{{isogashii|stem|忙[いそが]しく}}なければ、{{tetsudau|masu|手伝[てつだ]います}}。
```

*If I'm not busy, I'll help.*

**な-adjectives and nouns** don't take ば directly — there's no verb-like stem for it to grab onto, since these words lean on the copula だ instead of conjugating on their own. Instead, that だ turns into なら, which is casual and by far the most common choice, or into the more formal であれば, which you'll see more in writing and polite speech than in conversation.

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なら、{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}{{dekiru|masu|できます}}。
```

*If it's quiet, I can study.*

```jp
{{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}}であれば、{{yasui-adj||安[やす]い}}です。
```

*If you're a student, it's cheap.*

Look back at those examples and you'll notice ば never actually shows up by itself except right after a verb — {{suru|stem|せ}}ば、れば、{{suru|stem|すれ}}ば、ければ、なら、であれば are all the same idea, just wearing whatever shape the word in front of it demands. Once you can spot the base word hiding underneath the ending, none of these are a surprise anymore; you're not learning six patterns, you're learning one pattern with five outfits.

## Rules and exceptions

Here's the edge that catches almost everyone the first time through: when the ば clause describes an action rather than a state, the sentence can't end in a command, an invitation, or a "let's."

> `図書館に行けば、本を借りましょう` sounds broken to a native ear even though every piece is conjugated correctly. Swap the front clause to たら instead, and it becomes completely natural: {{toshokan||図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]}}に{{iku-v|stem|行[い]っ}}たら、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{kariru|stem|借[か]り}}ましょう。 ("Once you get to the library, let's borrow a book.")

It helps to have a reason, not just a rule to memorize: ば is stating something like a law of the world — a standing fact about how things work — and a law doesn't turn around and hand out orders in the same breath. たら, by contrast, is just narrating one step and then the next, so a command or invitation fits naturally after it.

That restriction lifts as soon as the front clause is a state instead of an action — an adjective, a negative, or a stative verb like {{wakaru||分[わ]かる}}. That's exactly why {{isogashii|stem|忙[いそが]しく}}なければ、{{tetsudau|masu|手伝[てつだ]います}} works without a hitch: {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} isn't an action, it's a description of how things are, and a description doesn't carry the same weight of "law" that an action does.

There's a second trap worth flagging: ければ only ever attaches to the plain form of an adjective. There's no polite version of the ending itself — you build it off {{takai-adj||高[たか]い}}, never off a -です or -ます shape of anything.

A third thing worth knowing: because ば describes a standing rule rather than one moment, it also does the job of a hypothetical — the "if I were, if I had" kind of if, about something that isn't true right now. The mechanics don't change at all; only the situation you're picturing does, and context usually makes clear which one you mean.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech, ければ often shrinks further, to けりゃ or even きゃ. {{takai-adj|stem|高[たか]けれ}}ば can turn into {{takai-adj|stem|高[たか]けりゃ}}, and {{isogashii|stem|忙[いそが]しけれ}}ば into {{isogashii|stem|忙[いそが]しけりゃ}}. It reads as blunt and a little rough around the edges, the kind of thing you'll hear from an older relative or in a casual drama more than from a coworker — worth recognizing when you hear it, not something you need to produce yet.

## Contrast: ば vs. たら

You already know たら for conditionals — Ta-form + ら. The two overlap enough on the surface to blur together, and honestly, in a lot of everyday sentences either one gets the point across and a native speaker won't blink. But they're answering different questions underneath. ば states a standing rule, something generally or always true; たら describes one specific event, usually something you're picturing as a single occurrence, often already decided by the time you're saying it.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|stem|降[ふ]れ}}ば、{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*If it rains, I stay home.*

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|stem|降[ふ]っ}}たら、{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*If it rains, I'll stay home.*

The English barely shifts, but the Japanese is telling two different stories. The first is a habit — rain, any rain, any day, and you're staying in, full stop, as a rule about yourself. The second is about one forecast, one day: if it rains today, that's what you'll do today, and tomorrow is a separate question. When you're talking about a single, particular event, たら is almost always the safer and more natural pick; save ば for the rule.

ので and のに aren't in this competition at all — they answer "why" and "even though," not "if" — so they don't overlap with ば the way たら does. It's easy to lump every because-shaped or if-shaped word together in your head early on, especially while all of them are still new; this is a good moment to let them separate back out into their own lanes.

You've actually already used なら twice above, quietly doing ば's job for nouns and な-adjectives. That's not the whole of what なら can do, though. On its own as a grammar point, なら can react to something someone just said, or raise a topic before you've even confirmed it's true — a job ば can't touch, since ば always states a rule rather than responding to the moment. Keep today's なら as one shape ば wears; the fuller version of it is still ahead of you.
caution_notes: Don't end a ば sentence with a command, invitation, or "let's" when the ば clause is a plain action verb — use たら there instead.
ければ only attaches to the plain form of an い-adjective (or the plain negative), never to a -です or -ます shape.
Use ば for a standing rule or general truth, not for one specific, already-decided event — that's what たら is for.
であれば and なら are the noun / な-adjective versions of ば; today's なら is not the same grammar point as the topic-based なら you'll meet later.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend corners you after class and says {{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}したいです — she wants to learn Japanese, and she's asking where to start. You already know exactly the book that got you through your first six months. This is the exact moment なら was built for: not a warning about some hypothetical future, the way English "if" so often is, but a direct reaction to the one thing she just put on the table.

Think about what actually happened in that exchange. She didn't hand you a condition to evaluate — she handed you a topic. Nothing in her sentence was uncertain to her; she wants to study Japanese, full stop. What's open is your response to that topic, and that's exactly the gap なら fills. English blurs this by using "if" for both jobs — real uncertainty ("if it rains") and simple topic-picking ("if it's Japanese you're after, try this book"). Japanese keeps a separate word for the second job, and this is it.

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}したいです。
```

*I want to study Japanese.*

You answer with {{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}なら、{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}が{{ii||いい}}ですよ。 Not "if you were to study Japanese, this book would be good" in some abstract sense — closer to "Japanese? Then this book." She names the topic, and なら lets you pick it straight up and react to it.

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}なら、{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}が{{ii||いい}}ですよ。
```

*If it's Japanese, this book is good.*

That's the whole shape of なら: someone puts an idea on the table — in words, or just by the situation you're both standing in — and なら is how you respond to that specific thing, not to conditions in general.

## How it works

{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}} in that sentence is a plain noun, and なら drops right onto it — no extra word in between, nothing to conjugate. That's the easiest case: **Noun + なら**. Whatever sits right before なら is the thing being reacted to, and everything after it is your answer to that one thing.

You already have an instinct for part of this. は marks a plain topic — {{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}は{{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}です says something true about Japanese in general. なら is what happens when that same topic-picking impulse turns conditional: instead of stating a fact about the topic, you're reacting to the topic having been raised at all. Same instinct, different job.

Verbs work the same way, just in their plain dictionary form. If your friend mentions a plan and you want to react to it directly:

```jp
{{iku-v||行[い]く}}なら、{{kippu||切[きっ]符[ぷ]}}を{{kau-v|stem|買[か]い}}ましょう。
```

*If you're going, let's buy the ticket.*

Nothing gets conjugated there — {{iku-v||行[い]く}} sits exactly as you'd find it in a dictionary, and なら just follows it.

な-adjectives are the one spot people trip on. Their plain form ends in だ ({{shizuka||静[しず]か}}だ — it's quiet), but なら doesn't want that だ at all — it replaces it:

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}だ → {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なら
```

*quiet → if it's quiet*

Drop the だ, attach なら directly. Skip that step and you get the very natural-looking but wrong `静かだなら` — an extra だ that shouldn't be there.

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なら、{{koko||ここ}}で{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}{{dekiru|masu|できます}}。
```

*If it's quiet, you can study here.*

い-adjectives don't have that problem. Their plain form already ends in い, so なら just tacks on with nothing to remove:

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}なら、{{tetsudau|stem|手伝[てつだ]い}}ましょうか。
```

*If you're busy, shall I help?*

And なら isn't stuck reacting to the present moment only. Past tense works too — た-form plus なら reacts to something that, as far as you know, already happened:

```jp
{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}なら、{{shashin||写[しゃ]真[しん]}}を{{miseru|te|見[み]せて}}ください。
```

*If you already went, show me the photos.*

Notice the shape holds steady across all of these: whatever form the premise takes — noun, い-adjective, な-adjective (だ dropped), plain verb, or ta-form — なら sits right after it, unchanged itself. All the flexibility lives in what comes before it.

## Rules and exceptions

Here's the part that's easy to get backwards. なら doesn't describe two events happening in order — first this occurs, then that occurs. It reacts to a premise, and that reaction can even land *before* the thing in the なら clause has actually happened. Telling your friend {{nihon||日本[にほん]}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}なら、{{kamera||カメラ}}が{{iru-need|masu|要[い]ります}}ね before she's booked a single ticket is completely normal — you're not narrating a future sequence, you're commenting on a topic she raised, right now.

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}なら、{{kamera||カメラ}}が{{iru-need|masu|要[い]ります}}ね。
```

*If you're going to Japan, you'll need a camera.*

> Even the negative version works the same way — {{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}なら (if you're not going) reacts to the same kind of stated premise, not to a future event that fails to occur. なら doesn't care whether the thing actually happens; it only cares that it was raised.

Where people usually reach for なら and get it wrong is when they actually mean "and then" — one action leading straight into the next as a timeline. That's not なら's job. Hold that thought; it's exactly where the contrast section below picks up.

There's also a very natural register this pattern lives in: giving advice or a recommendation on the spot, right after someone tells you something. Native speakers reach for なら constantly in exactly that moment — a friend mentions a plan, a problem, a preference, and なら is how you hand back a suggestion that's clearly tied to what they just said, rather than a generic piece of advice floating free of the conversation.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, plain-form + なら often tightens into んなら. That ん used to be の — the little word that turns a whole idea into "the thing where…" so you can treat it as a single unit and react to it — worn down by fast, casual speech into ん. {{iku-v||行[い]く}}のなら becomes {{iku-v||行[い]く}}んなら, and it usually carries a slightly more personal, "oh, since that's how it is" flavor than the plain version.

```jp
{{iku-v||行[い]く}}んなら、{{boku||僕[ぼく]}}も{{iku-v|stem|行[い]き}}たいです。
```

*If you're going, I want to go too.*

You'll hear んなら constantly between friends and almost never in writing or anything polite — keep plain なら for anything formal, and save んなら for conversation. If you've noticed わからない shrink into わかんない in the same kind of relaxed speech, this is the same instinct at work: a longer, more explanatory shape wearing down into something quicker once both people already know what's being talked about.

## Contrast

You already have three other conditional-shaped tools, and なら doesn't compete with them so much as sit in its own lane.

たら describes a sequence: this happens, and then that follows. Compare your ticket-buying line from earlier with this one:

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}に{{iku-v|stem|行[い]っ}}たら、{{shashin||写[しゃ]真[しん]}}を{{okuru|masu|送[おく]ります}}。
```

*When I go to Japan, I'll send photos.*

That's a straight timeline — arrival first, photo-sending after, in that order. Swap in なら for the same sentence and it stops being a timeline entirely; it turns into a reaction to the fact that Japan is even on the table as a topic, with no promise about what happens first.

ば behaves more like a general-truth switch than a reaction to something said. It describes conditions and results with less regard for who mentioned what to whom — it's built for patterns that hold true in general, not for responding to a specific thing your friend just told you. なら, by contrast, only makes sense once something has actually been raised. You can't なら a fact nobody put on the table.

ので is a different animal altogether — it explains a reason, not a condition. {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}ので{{tetsudau|masu|手伝[てつだ]いません}} tells you *why* something is true: because you're busy, you won't help. {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}なら{{tetsudau|masu|手伝[てつだ]います}} tells you what you'll do *if* that turns out to be the situation. Reason versus reaction — the two can look similar on the page, but don't let that fool you; swapping one for the other changes what the sentence is actually claiming.

Line them all up against the same friend mentioning she's busy this week, and the differences stop being abstract. たら would describe her getting busy and then something following from it, in that order. ば would describe busyness as a general condition with a general result, no particular friend required. ので would explain busyness as the reason behind something else that's true. なら is the only one of the four that's actually built to react to her having said it — which is exactly why it's the one you reach for most often in ordinary conversation.

The test for なら, every time, is simple: did someone just put something on the table — a plan, a fact, a topic? If so, なら is how you pick it up and answer it directly. Once you meet the can-do form later on, you'll find it pairing with なら constantly — whether something's even possible is just one more thing worth reacting to.
caution_notes: なら reacts to something already said or already known — it is not for two events happening one after another in time, which is たら's job.
な-adjectives and nouns drop だ before なら — 静かだなら keeps an extra だ that does not belong there.
んなら is a casual contraction of のなら used in conversation — avoid it in polite or written Japanese.
Past tense + なら still reacts to a stated premise; it does not turn the sentence into a strict before-and-after sequence.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend wants to go to the beach this weekend, and already has the whole day sketched out — towels, a cooler, maybe a nap on the sand afterward. Before anyone agrees to any of it, there's one practical question standing between you and actually getting in the water.

```jp
{{oyogeru||泳[およ]げる}}？
```

*Can you swim?*

That ending isn't a new verb — it's {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}} (to swim) wearing a different outfit. Japanese has a whole conjugation dedicated to exactly this idea: not "I swim" but "I'm capable of swimming, if it comes to that." It's called the potential form, and once you can build it, you can ask and answer this kind of question about almost anything you already know how to do — not just what you're doing, but what's within your reach to do.

{{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}} on its own just states an action: someone swims, or is swimming, or will swim. {{oyogeru||泳[およ]げる}} doesn't state an action at all — it states a standing fact about you, true whether or not you ever actually get in the water this weekend. That's the whole difference between the plain form and the potential form: one reports what happens, the other reports what's possible.

## How it works

The potential form replaces the ending of a verb with れる or られる, attached to the stem — everything before that final る. Which ending you use, and how much of the verb survives the swap, depends on which of three families the verb belongs to. You've already been sorting verbs into these families without necessarily naming them; this is just the first time the split actually changes which ending you reach for.

Ichidan verbs — the ones whose dictionary form always ends in an e-sound or i-sound plus る, like {{taberu||食[た]べる}} or {{miru-v||見[み]る}} — are the easy case. Drop that final る and add られる, and you're done. {{miru-v||見[み]る}} becomes {{mirareru||見[み]られる}}, {{okiru||起[お]きる}} becomes {{okiru|stem|起[お]き}}られる, and the pattern never wobbles.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}}
```

*to eat -> can eat*

So if the food at your friend's place turns out fierier than expected, you can still hold your own, and say so without changing anything else about the sentence.

```jp
{{karai||辛[から]い}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}も{{taberareru||食[た]べられる}}。
```

*I can even eat spicy food.*

Godan verbs — the ones like {{kau-v||買[か]う}} or {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} whose ending actually shifts shape depending on what follows it — do this differently, and it's worth slowing down for. The final u-sound moves back to an e-sound, and る attaches directly, with no られる involved at all. {{kaku||書[か]く}} becomes {{kakeru-write-potential||書[か]ける}}, {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} becomes {{nomeru||飲[の]める}}, and {{kau-v||買[か]う}} (to buy) becomes {{kaeru-potential||買[か]える}}.

```jp
{{kau-v||買[か]う}} → {{kaeru-potential||買[か]える}}
```

*to buy -> can buy*

Same shift, any object you can name.

```jp
{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}が{{kaeru-potential||買[か]える}}。
```

*I can buy an umbrella.*

This is also why {{hanaseru||話[はな]せる}} already sits in your vocabulary as "can speak" — it was never a separate word to memorize in the first place. It's {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} run through this exact same shift, and once you see it that way, a handful of other "-eru" words you already know will start looking less like arbitrary vocabulary and more like verbs you'd already half-learned.

The two irregular verbs go their own way, and neither borrows the regular ichidan or godan pattern. {{suru||する}} becomes {{dekiru||できる}}, not `すれる` — an irregular jump you've probably already met as its own vocabulary word, long before you needed the grammar behind it. {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} becomes {{koreru||来[こ]られる}}, borrowing the ichidan ending even though {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} itself isn't ichidan.

```jp
{{kuru-v||来[く]る}} → {{koreru||来[こ]られる}}
```

*to come -> can come*

Which means when your friend circles back with the actual invitation, the grammar is already sitting in your hands, fully built.

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}、{{koreru||来[こ]られる}}？
```

*Can you come this weekend?*

## Rules and exceptions

One habit worth building early: potential-form sentences usually mark what you're able to do with が, not を. {{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}が{{hanaseru||話[はな]せる}}, not `日本語を話せる` — you'll hear the second version in relaxed speech, and older textbooks sometimes treat it as acceptable too, but が is the one to default to until you have a feel for when the looser version fits. Some speakers reach for を when the sentence already has a strong sense of "doing something to this specific thing," but that's a nuance to notice later, not a reason to second-guess が now.

> Two words you already know look like they might be potential forms of verbs you've met, and neither one is. {{mieru||見[み]える}} ("to be visible") is not the potential of {{miru-v||見[み]る}} — that would be {{mirareru||見[み]られる}}. {{kikoeru||聞[き]こえる}} ("to be audible") is not the potential of {{kiku-v||聞[き]く}} — that would be 聞[き]ける. Both describe something reaching you on its own, not your ability to perceive it, and mixing them up is one of the most common slips at this level, precisely because the two pairs look like they should line up and don't.

{{dekiru||できる}} is worth one more note. It started life as {{suru||する}}'s potential form, but it's drifted into being the everyday word for "possible" or "can," used on its own the way English uses *can* — you'll see it standing alone in sentences that have nothing to do with {{suru||する}} at all. That's a normal fate for a potential form popular enough to become a vocabulary word in its own right — it happened to a handful of others too, which is exactly why {{hanaseru||話[はな]せる}} was already sitting in your list before this lesson.

One more thing worth knowing before you go further: once you've built a potential form, it behaves exactly like a brand-new ichidan verb from that point on. {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} conjugates like {{taberu||食[た]べる}}'s cousin, not like the original {{taberu||食[た]べる}} — so every negative, past tense, or conditional you build on top of it follows ichidan rules, regardless of which family the original verb came from. That detail is what makes the contrast section below work at all. It also means the negative follows the same ichidan pattern: {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}}'s negative is {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}られない, built the same way you'd negate {{mirareru||見[み]られる}} or any other ichidan verb, with nothing extra to learn.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, ichidan potential forms routinely drop a syllable in the middle. {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} becomes 食[た]べれる — the ら quietly disappears, and nobody blinks.

```jp
{{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} → 食[た]べれる
```

*can eat -> can eat (casual)*

> This dropping only touches ichidan potential forms — the ones built with られる in the first place. Godan forms like {{kaeru-potential||買[か]える}} or {{oyogeru||泳[およ]げる}} never had a ら to lose, so there's no shortcut to take there. Formal writing and most tests still expect the full られる, and some listeners quietly judge the short version, so treat it as something to recognize on sight before you lean on it yourself.

## Contrast: なら and たら with a potential verb

Once a verb sits in potential form, you'll find it slotting into conditionals you already know — and which one you pick still changes the sentence, even though the potential half stays identical. なら reacts to something already on the table: someone hands you a fact, and なら responds to it directly, almost like the second half of a conversation someone else started.

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}が{{hanaseru||話[はな]せる}}なら、{{benri||便[べん]利[り]}}だ。
```

*If you can speak Japanese, that's convenient.*

Swap in たら, and the sentence stops reacting to a given fact and starts describing a future checkpoint instead — first this becomes true, then that follows, in that order.

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}が{{hanaseru|stem|話[はな]せ}}たら、{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}が{{tanoshii||楽[たの]しい}}。
```

*Once you can speak Japanese, travel gets fun.*

Say the なら version and you sound like you're responding to someone who just told you they can speak Japanese. Say the たら version and you sound like you're picturing a future where that's true and imagining what comes after. Same potential verb, same conditional-sounding grammar, genuinely different scene in the listener's head.

The shape doesn't change here — れる and られる will look exactly the same whether the topic is ability or, soon, something being done to you instead of by you. There's no shortcut for telling them apart except context: who's doing what to whom, and whether the sentence is describing a capability or an event landing on someone. Hold onto that; passive voice borrows this exact conjugation next, and sorting the two apart is the hurdle waiting right after this one.
caution_notes: Potential-form sentences usually mark the thing you can do with が, not を — 日本語が話せる is the default, even though the を version shows up in casual speech.
見える and 聞こえる are their own vocabulary words, not the potential forms of 見る and 聞く, which are actually 見られる and 聞ける.
Casual speech often drops the ら from ichidan potential forms (食べられる → 食べれる), but formal writing and most tests still expect the full form.
する's potential form is the irregular できる, not すれる.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your teacher hands back your essay with a note in the margin, and later you're telling a friend how it went. In English you'd probably say "my teacher praised me" — but Japanese has an instinct that flips the sentence around, putting you in the position of receiving the action instead of your teacher in the position of giving it.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{homeru|stem|褒[ほ]め}}られました。
```

*I was praised by my teacher.*

That's the passive: something happens to the subject of the sentence, and whoever's doing it gets marked with に instead of standing at the front as the subject. Once you can build れる・られる, you can talk about getting complimented, getting your things borrowed, even getting rained on — every situation where you're on the receiving end rather than the one acting. English usually needs "was" plus a past participle to do this; Japanese does it with one verb ending.

## How it works

The passive attaches to the verb stem, and which stem you use depends on the verb's group — the same three-way split you already learned for the potential form. The idea behind all three groups is the same: take the verb, shift it into a stem that no longer commits to a subject deciding to act, and let れる or られる mark that something simply occurred, with you or someone else on the receiving end.

### Ichidan verbs

Drop the final る and add られる.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}}
```

*to eat → to be eaten*

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{pan||パン}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}られた。
```

*My bread got eaten by my little brother.*

Notice something odd there: {{pan||パン}} still has を on it, exactly the marker it would carry in the plain sentence {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}が{{pan||パン}}を{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}} (my brother ate the bread). The passive didn't promote {{pan||パン}} to subject — it just layered "and this happened to me" on top of the original sentence. Hold onto that; it matters again in a minute.

Once you notice the shape, you'll see it everywhere: {{mirareru||見[み]られる}} (to be seen), {{oshieru|stem|教[おし]え}}られる (to be taught), {{wasureru|stem|忘[わす]れ}}られる (to be forgotten) are all the exact same stem+られる move, no extra mechanics required.

### Godan verbs

Take the verb's final う-row sound, shift it back one row to あ, and add れる.

```jp
{{yomu||読[よ]む}} → {{yomu|stem|読[よ]ま}}れる
```

*to read → to be read*

```jp
{{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}が{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ま}}れた。
```

*The letter was read.*

This one has no に anywhere — nobody's named as the reader. That's normal for a godan passive describing an event rather than a grievance: the letter got read, full stop, and who did the reading isn't the point.

Verbs ending in う are the one spot where this shift looks strange, because う doesn't have a matching あ-row sound to fall back on — it borrows わ instead.

```jp
{{tsukau||使[つか]う}} → {{tsukau|stem|使[つか]わ}}れる
```

*to use → to be used*

You've actually met this あ-row shift before: it's the same vowel step you use to build the negative. {{yomu||読[よ]む}} becomes {{yomu|nai|読[よ]まない}} the same way it becomes {{yomu|stem|読[よ]ま}}れる — once you can build one, the muscle memory for the other is already there. The same pattern covers {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} → {{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]さ}}れる and {{yobu||呼[よ]ぶ}} → {{yobu|stem|呼[よ]ば}}れる without anything new to learn.

### Irregular verbs

{{suru||する}} and {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} don't follow either pattern; you just have to know them.

```jp
{{suru||する}} → {{suru|stem|さ}}れる
```

*to do → to be done*

```jp
{{kuru-v||来[く]る}} → {{koreru||来[こ]られる}}
```

*to come → to have someone come*

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}に{{kuru-v|stem|来[こ]}}られた。
```

*A friend came over on me, and it was inconvenient.*

That last one is the strangest sentence in this lesson if you translate it word for word, because English won't let you passivize "come" — nobody "gets come to." Japanese doesn't care. れる・られる isn't reserved for things being done to an object; it can mark that an event, even one nobody aimed at you, landed on you and cost you something.

> The passive on an intransitive verb like {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} or {{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}} almost always signals mild inconvenience. {{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}に{{kuru-v|stem|来[こ]}}られた reads less like "a friend visited" and more like "I got visited on, and it threw off my evening."

## Rules and exceptions

に marks whoever performed the action — the teacher who praised you, the brother who ate your bread. Drop it and the sentence becomes a plain, agentless description of something happening, exactly what {{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}が{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ま}}れた is doing. You'll drop it constantly: most passive sentences you'll actually use skip the agent, because either it's obvious from context or naming it would sound oddly pointed, almost like an accusation.

The を you saw stay put in {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{pan||パン}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}られた is a real exception, not a typo. When the passive expresses something being done to your belongings rather than to you directly, the item keeps its を and you keep your ordinary subject slot (an implied {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は here). Force the item into が instead — `パンが食べられた` — and you get a completely different, agentless sentence about bread going missing, not about your brother's crime.

> For ichidan verbs and for {{kuru-v||来[く]る}}, the passive and the potential share the exact same conjugation. {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} can mean "gets eaten" or "can eat" depending on nothing the verb itself tells you — only the sentence around it decides.

Don't reach for れる・られる just because an English sentence happens to be passive. "The window was broken" usually sounds more natural in Japanese as an active or plain statement unless you specifically need to flag that someone was affected by it — this pattern exists for when being affected is the whole point.

That's also why the passive shows up so often around family and friends rather than strangers and objects: {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{pan||パン}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}られた only makes sense as a sentence because your bread going missing is *your* problem, not an abstract fact about the world. Compare that to {{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}が{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ま}}れた, where nobody's inconvenience is on the table — just an event, reported plainly.

## Contrast: passive vs. potential

You already know れる・られる as the potential form, and the shape really is identical — which is exactly why context has to do the work the verb itself can't. There's a reason the two share a form: both describe the subject *not* being the one driving the action — either the action simply becomes possible on its own, or it simply happens to someone. English treats those as two unrelated grammar categories; Japanese never bothered to split them.

```jp
{{kore||これ}}は{{taberareru||食[た]べられる}}？
```

*Can this be eaten?*

Nothing here is happening to anyone; nobody's marked with に, and the whole sentence is asking about a quality of {{kore||これ}} rather than reporting an event. That's the tell: potential sentences ask about ability or possibility and rarely carry an agent acting on someone, while passive sentences almost always have — or clearly imply — someone whose action lands on someone else.

You'll also hear ら-less shortcuts like `食べれる` in casual speech. That belongs to the potential only — dropping ら is never done for the passive, so {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} keeps its full form no matter how casual the conversation gets.

So the real question with any れる・られる sentence isn't just "can I build this," it's "what's actually happening to whom." Keep that question in mind and the two readings stop colliding — you'll find yourself scanning for an agent and a に before you even finish reading the sentence.

This shape isn't done evolving, either. Fuse it with the causative later and you get {{suru|stem|せ}}られる・{{suru|stem|さ}}せられる, the "made to do it against your will" pattern, which takes exactly the inconvenience you just met in {{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}に{{kuru-v|stem|来[こ]}}られた and turns the volume all the way up.
caution_notes: The passive can attach to intransitive verbs like 来る and 降る to show an event landed on you against your will, and this 'adversity' reading has no direct English equivalent, so avoid translating it word for word.
For ichidan verbs and 来る, the passive form is identical to the potential form — only the surrounding context tells you which meaning is intended.
When the passive describes something happening to your belongings rather than to you, the item can stay marked with を instead of becoming the subject with が — don't rewrite it to が.
Not every English passive sentence should become れる・られる in Japanese; use it only when someone being affected by the action is actually the point.
items.mnemonic_text: At the riverbank, a duck bumps Ken the dog into the water. He climbs out dripping and growls "<reading>Rail</reading>roaded!": that was <grammar>done to him</grammar>. {{otouto||弟}}に{{warau|stem|笑わ}}<reading>れる</reading>。

items.explanation_markdown:
Your little brother is staring at a plate of vegetables like it personally insulted him. You've tried asking nicely. You've tried bargaining. Tonight you're done negotiating — he's going to eat them, whether he likes it or not. English hands you one verb, "make," and expects tone of voice to do the rest. Japanese hands you a whole new verb form built for exactly this moment.

That form is the causative — a version of the verb that puts *you* in charge of someone else's action instead of describing your own. Where {{taberu||食[た]べる}} means "eat," {{taberasaseru||食[た]べさせる}} means "make (someone) eat" — or, in gentler situations, "let (someone) eat." Same ending, two very different dinners.

```jp
{{haha||母[はは]}}は{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberasaseru||食[た]べさせる}}。
```

*Mother makes her little brother eat vegetables.*

You'll hear this shape constantly from whoever gets to call the shots in a given relationship — parents, teachers, doctors, bosses. It isn't rude on its own; it's just the grammar of someone directing someone else's action, the way "have someone do something" works in English. Whether the mood underneath is a stern order or a small kindness is a separate question, one you'll unpack a little further down.

## How it works

The causative attaches to the same verb stem you already know from potential and passive — you're not learning a new attachment point, just a new thing to attach.

For an ichidan verb (the ones ending in an -eru or -iru you can just drop), knock off る and add させる:

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberasaseru||食[た]べさせる}}
```

*to eat → to make (someone) eat*

For a godan verb, shift the final syllable back from the "u" row to the "a" row, then add せる — the exact same vowel shift you already did for potential and passive, just with a different auxiliary bolted on:

```jp
{{iku-v||行[い]く}} → {{ikaseru||行[い]かせる}}
```

*to go → to make (someone) go*

The two irregulars don't follow either pattern, so they're just worth memorizing outright:

```jp
{{suru||する}} → させる
```

*to do → to make (someone) do*

```jp
{{kuru-v||来[く]る}} → {{kuru-v|stem|来[き]}}させる
```

*to come → to make (someone) come*

> {{kuru-v|stem|来[き]}}させる looks like plain {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} with させる stuck on, but the reading underneath shifts — {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} is くる, while {{kuru-v|stem|来[き]}}させる is こさせる. It's the same quirk you've already met in {{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]ない}} (こない); the kanji stays put, the reading moves.

Once you've built the causative verb, it behaves like any other verb ending in -eru — it takes ます, ない, た, all the endings you already use every day. {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させます, {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させない, {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させた. Nothing new to learn there.

That {{suru||する}} rule pays off well beyond the bare verb "to do." Every noun-plus-{{suru||する}} verb you know — {{souji-suru||掃[そう]除[じ]する}}, {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}, {{renshuu-suru||練[れん]習[しゅう]する}} — swaps its {{suru||する}} for させる the exact same way: {{souji-suru|stem|掃[そう]除[じ]さ}}せる, {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}させる, {{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]さ}}せる. You've already memorized dozens of these nouns; you're not adding new vocabulary, just reusing the one irregular conjugation across all of them.

The one genuinely new decision is which particle marks the person being made to act. It depends on whether the verb is *transitive* — one that takes a direct object, like {{taberu||食[た]べる}} (eat *something*) — or *intransitive*, one that doesn't, like {{hashiru||走[はし]る}} (run). With a transitive verb, the object keeps its を and the person doing the acting gets に, same as sentence one above: {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を. With an intransitive verb, there's no object competing for を, so the person takes it instead.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}は{{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}}を{{hashiru|stem|走[はし]ら}}せる。
```

*The teacher makes the students run.*

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せる。
```

*I make my little brother drink the medicine.*

Notice {{hashiru||走[はし]る}} has nobody else to give を to, so {{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}} takes it. {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} already has {{kusuri||薬[くすり]}} sitting on を, so {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}} gets に instead. Once you see the object competing for the particle, the split stops feeling arbitrary — check whether the verb already needs a を, and hand the leftover particle to whoever's being made to act.

This scales to any verb you already know without extra memorizing. {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} has an object (you speak *something*), so its causee takes に. {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}} doesn't, so its causee takes を. You're not learning a new fact per verb — you're just asking the one question you already know how to answer from ordinary sentences: does this verb take an object or not?

## Rules and exceptions

Nothing in the grammar itself tells you whether a causative sentence is bossy or generous — that's entirely down to context. The same structure that forces your brother to eat vegetables can just as easily describe a parent being soft.

```jp
{{haha||母[はは]}}は{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}を{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}で{{asobu|stem|遊[あそ]ば}}せる。
```

*Mother lets her child play in the park.*

Nobody has to twist a child's arm to get them into a park. Swap the scene to homework and the identical grammar reads as strict instead of kind — the sentence doesn't change; your mental picture of the situation does.

> The single most common slip is dropping the さ on an ichidan verb — writing `食べせる` instead of {{taberasaseru||食[た]べさせる}}. Ichidan causatives are always -させる, never a bare -せる; the shorter form only happens on godan verbs, where せる is already doing all the work after the vowel shift.

The causee particle rule has no exceptions worth worrying about, but it does have one boundary worth stating outright: whatever the verb, the person being made or allowed to act is never marked with が. That particle stays reserved for the thing someone wants, likes, or is capable of — categories that belong to entirely different patterns, not this one. If you find が creeping into a causative sentence, you've drifted into potential without meaning to.

Because the causative puts you above someone else in the sentence, it can land harshly if you aim it at a superior — a boss, a teacher, someone older. Softening that is a matter of surrounding vocabulary and tone rather than a rule the grammar itself enforces, so for now, just notice that the bare causative describes *who's directing whom*, not how anyone involved feels about it.

## Contrast

You've actually met れる・られる twice already — once for potential, once for passive — and both times it attached to the same stem you're using now. せる・させる sits right next to them structurally, which is exactly why it's easy to blur the three together under pressure. The fix is remembering who the sentence is about: potential and passive both put the subject on the receiving end of the verb; causative puts the subject in the driver's seat, making the action happen *to* someone else.

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}は{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}が{{taberareru||食[た]べられる}}。
```

*My little brother can eat vegetables.*

{{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} and {{taberasaseru||食[た]べさせる}} are one vowel apart and mean almost opposite things — one says he's capable of it, the other says somebody's forcing the issue. When you catch yourself unsure which one you meant, ask who's actually chewing. If it's the subject of the sentence, you want potential. If the subject is pulling strings from outside the action, you want causative. Notice, too, that {{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}} sits on が in the potential sentence and on を in the causative one — the particle swap you just learned to spot for causees works as a quiet tell for which pattern you're looking at.

The same test travels to any verb pair you already know. Take {{hashiru|stem|走[はし]ら}}せる from earlier: swap さ for れ and you'd be saying the student is capable of running, {{hashireru||走[はし]れる}}, not that anyone ordered him onto the track. The vowel is the whole difference between an ability and an instruction.

Sometimes the two even stack: someone gets made to do something, and *they're* the one stuck experiencing it rather than causing it. That flip side — being on the receiving end of somebody else's causative — gets its own form soon: {{suru|stem|せ}}られる・{{suru|stem|さ}}せられる, the causative-passive. Today's job is just getting comfortable putting other people in the driver's seat you're steering from. The version where somebody else steers *you* can wait.
caution_notes: Mixing up causative せる／させる with potential／passive れる・られる produces a real but wrong-meaning verb, so always check who is actually performing the action.
Ichidan verbs always take させる, never a bare せる — writing 食べせる instead of 食べさせる is the single most common slip.
Whether a causative sentence reads as forceful or permissive is decided entirely by context, not by the grammar itself.
The causee's particle depends on whether the verb is transitive (に) or intransitive (を), and it is never marked with が.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend tops up your glass. You already said you were done, you meant it, and the glass is full again anyway. The next morning someone asks how the night went, and none of the sentences you own quite fit. {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} is true, but it makes the whole evening sound like your project. A sentence with your friend as the subject puts the spotlight on them, when the story is really about what happened to you.

This is the sentence you want:

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}に{{osake||お酒[さけ]}}を飲[の]まされる。
```

*My friend makes me drink.*

飲[の]まされる is two forms you already have, welded together. You know {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せる, the causative — the make-or-let form. You know {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}れる, the passive — the form where the action lands on you rather than starting from you. Stack the passive on top of the causative and you get the form for sitting on the wrong end of somebody else's decision: they decided, your body carried it out, and you would rather it hadn't.

That last part is not decoration. This pattern is not neutral, the way English "I was asked to" is neutral. Built into it is the fact that you didn't want to. A speaker who chooses this form is complaining — mildly, maybe fondly, but complaining.

## How it works

Two moves, always in this order: build the causative first, then make that causative passive.

Start with a る-verb (ichidan — the ones that simply drop る). {{taberu||食[た]べる}} goes to causative {{taberasaseru||食[た]べさせる}}, and then the せる ending swaps to せられる.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させられる
```

*to eat → to be made to eat*

Put it to work on the child who has strong opinions about dinner:

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}は{{maiban||毎[まい]晩[ばん]}}{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させられる。
```

*Every night my little brother is made to eat his vegetables.*

う-verbs (godan) take the same two steps, plus a shortcut the language worked out for you a long time ago. {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} goes to {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せる, and that goes to {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せられる. Four syllables of ending is a lot to carry, so {{suru|stem|せ}}られ got squeezed down to {{suru|stem|さ}}れ.

```jp
{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} → {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せられる → 飲[の]まされる
```

*to drink → to be made to drink (long form) → to be made to drink (short form)*

Both are correct Japanese. The long {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せられる is what the textbook builds and what you meet in careful writing; the short 飲[の]まされる is what people actually say, and it is the one that will come flying at you in conversation. Recognize both. Produce whichever one you can assemble faster under pressure — nobody will mark you down.

The two irregular verbs behave themselves. {{suru||する}} becomes させられる and {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} becomes {{kuru-v|stem|来[き]}}させられる. Every {{suru||する}}-verb inherits this automatically, so {{souji-suru||掃[そう]除[じ]する}} gives {{souji-suru|stem|掃[そう]除[じ]さ}}せられる, {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}} gives {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}させられる, and so on down the list.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{nichiyoubi||日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]}}に{{souji-suru|stem|掃[そう]除[じ]さ}}せられる。
```

*On Sundays I get put to work cleaning.*

Now the particles, which you can borrow wholesale from the passive. The person who made it happen takes に — the friend with the bottle, the teacher with the worksheet. The thing the action lands on keeps を. And you, the one whose hands and mouth actually did the unwanted thing, are the topic or subject: は or が.

The shape, then, is: victim は instigator に object を verb.

## Rules and exceptions

The short form has one hard limit: it belongs to う-verbs only, and only to those that don't end in す. {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} builds its causative as {{hanashi||話[はなし]}}{{suru|stem|さ}}せる, so the causative-passive is {{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]さ}}せられる. Contracting that would hand you `話さされる`, with さ crashing into さ, and Japanese simply refuses.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}で{{eigo||英[えい]語[ご]}}を{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]さ}}せられる。
```

*At meetings I'm the one who gets made to speak English.*

> Never contract an ichidan verb either. `食べさされる` is not a form. る-verbs and す-verbs use the long ending, full stop.

{{matsu||待[ま]つ}} deserves its own line, because {{matasareru||待[ま]たされる}} is one of the highest-frequency members of this entire family. Waiting is the classic thing that gets done to a person.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{eki||駅[えき]}}で一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]{{matasareru||待[ま]たされる}}。
```

*I get left waiting at the station for an hour.*

Notice how the English drifts there. "Made to wait" is stiff; "kept waiting" is what an English speaker actually says. Expect that. The Japanese form is one consistent thing, but the natural English for it changes verb by verb, and chasing a single English formula will make your translations worse, not better.

> される on its own is also the plain passive of {{suru||する}}. So {{souji-suru|stem|掃[そう]除[じ]さ}}れる means something got cleaned — nobody was forced into anything. If you mean a person was put to work, you need the extra syllable: {{souji-suru|stem|掃[そう]除[じ]さ}}せられる.

One more edge, and this one is social rather than mechanical. Because the pattern carries a complaint, you don't use it for things you chose, even unpleasant ones. Stayed late for {{zangyou||残[ざん]業[ぎょう]}} because you decided the work needed finishing? Plain sentence. Stayed late because the office kept you there? The causative-passive is exactly right, and everyone hearing it will pick up the resentment without you adding a single extra word.

## Casual speech

The contraction above *is* casual speech doing its work, and in conversation it goes further: the plain forms crowd out the polite ones. Among friends you'll hear 飲[の]まされる and 飲[の]まされた far more often than {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せられます, and the long {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せられた can land as slightly formal, or as someone deliberately slowing down to make a point of it.

For ichidan and す-verbs there's no shortcut available, so casual speech just strips the politeness instead: {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させられた, {{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]さ}}せられた, {{souji-suru|stem|掃[そう]除[じ]さ}}せられた. The ending stays long because it has nowhere shorter to go.

## Contrast

Here is the minimal triple. Same two people, same beer, three grammars, three completely different stories.

First, the causative you already know. Your older brother is the one making decisions:

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{watashi||私[わたし]}}に{{biiru||ビール}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せる。
```

*My older brother makes me drink beer.*

Now the plain passive. Same brother, but nobody is forcing anybody — the beer was yours, he drank it, and the sentence exists because you're annoyed:

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{ani||兄[あに]}}に{{biiru||ビール}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}れる。
```

*My brother goes and drinks my beer on me.*

And the causative-passive, where you are the subject just like in the passive, but this time the beer went down your throat:

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{ani||兄[あに]}}に{{biiru||ビール}}を飲[の]まされる。
```

*My brother makes me drink beer.*

Hold the first and the third side by side. They report one single event from two different seats. {{ani||兄[あに]}} has the plan in both of them; what changes is who the sentence is about and whose experience we're being told. Swap them by accident and you've just claimed to be the one pouring.

There's a bonus here, and it's rare enough to be worth pointing out. {{taberareru||食[た]べられる}} has to work three jobs at once — passive, potential, and polite — and you disambiguate it from context. {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}させられる has no such problem. However long it is, it means exactly one thing, every time. The length is the price of the clarity.

## A closing thought

Causative plus passive, in that order, with に on whoever is responsible and you as the topic — and a built-in shrug of complaint that you can't switch off. Keep half an eye on the fact that being made to do something for long enough tends to end somewhere else entirely: there's a pattern coming, ように{{naru-become||なる}}, for the moment a thing you couldn't do becomes a thing you just do.
caution_notes: The shortened ending belongs only to う-verbs that do not end in す; ichidan verbs and す-verbs keep the long ending.
話す gives 話させられる and never `話さされる`, because two さ in a row is blocked.
される alone is also the plain passive of する, so 掃除される means something got cleaned while 掃除させられる means a person got put to work.
The person responsible is marked with に, and the form always carries a note of complaint — if the choice was yours, use a plain sentence instead.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've taped a note to the fridge door and you're halfway through writing it when you remember who's going to read it: a six-year-old. So you start over and make the letters twice as big.

Nothing about *what* you wrote changed. What changed is the reason behind how you wrote it — and that reason isn't a word, it's a whole little sentence: *so that the kid can read it*. Japanese hangs that sentence in front of the main one and glues it on with ように.

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}にも{{yomeru||読[よ]める}}ように、{{ookii|stem|大[おお]きく}}{{kaku|masu|書[か]きました}}。
```

*I wrote it big so that even a child could read it.*

{{yomeru||読[よ]める}} is the potential form you already know — *can read*. Everything before ように is the situation you're aiming at. Everything after it is what you actually did to get there. The comma is doing real work: it's the seam between goal and action.

## How it works

ように attaches to a plain, non-past verb. That's two options: dictionary form ({{yomeru||読[よ]める}}, {{kikoeru||聞[き]こえる}}, {{wakaru||分[わ]かる}}) when you want something to happen, or ない form ({{okureru|nai|遅[おく]れない}}, {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}, {{hairu-v|nai|入[はい]らない}}) when you want something *not* to happen. Then a comma, then the thing you did or will do.

The negative version is at least as common as the positive one, and it's usually the first one learners actually need — most of daily life is arranging things so a small disaster doesn't occur.

```jp
{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}に{{okureru|nai|遅[おく]れない}}ように、{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{ie||家[いえ]}}を{{deru-v|masu|出[で]ました}}。
```

*I left home early so that I wouldn't be late for the train.*

Look at {{okureru|nai|遅[おく]れない}}. It's plain, even though the sentence ends politely with {{deru-v|masu|出[で]ました}}. That's not sloppiness — it's the rule. More on that in a moment.

Now the part that decides whether your sentences sound native or slightly off: **the verb in front of ように is normally something nobody directly controls.** Potential forms live here happily ({{yomeru||読[よ]める}}, {{kikoeru||聞[き]こえる}}, {{mieru||見[み]える}}, {{dekiru||できる}}, {{wakaru||分[わ]かる}}), and so do intransitive verbs — verbs that describe something simply happening rather than someone doing it to something ({{hairu-v||入[はい]る}}, {{okureru||遅[おく]れる}}, {{tomaru||止[と]まる}}, {{nakunaru||無[な]くなる}}).

```jp
{{minna||みんな}}に{{kikoeru||聞[き]こえる}}ように、{{ookii||大[おお]きい}}{{koe||声[こえ]}}で{{hanasu-v|masu|話[はな]しました}}。
```

*I spoke in a loud voice so that everyone could hear.*

{{kikoeru||聞[き]こえる}} is *to be audible* — you can't order someone's ears to work. You can only adjust your voice and hope. That gap between "what I can do" and "what I want to come about" is exactly the space ように fills.

That also means the two halves of the sentence often have **different subjects**, which surprises people the first time.

```jp
{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{hairu-v|nai|入[はい]らない}}ように、{{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{shimeru|masu|閉[し]めます}}。
```

*I'll close the window so that the cat doesn't get in.*

The cat is the one entering; you're the one closing. Two people (well, one person and one cat) in one sentence, and Japanese doesn't mind at all. This is typical, not an edge case.

```jp
{{inu||犬[いぬ]}}が{{mizu||水[みず]}}を{{nomeru||飲[の]める}}ように、{{sara||皿[さら]}}を{{niwa||庭[にわ]}}に{{oku|masu|置[お]きました}}。
```

*I put a dish in the garden so the dog could drink water.*

Same shape: dog drinks, you place. Potential form before ように, deliberate action after it.

And when the subject *is* the same on both sides, the verb before ように is still something outside your direct command:

```jp
{{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}ように、{{nooto||ノート}}に{{kaku|masu|書[か]きます}}。
```

*I write it in my notebook so I won't forget.*

You can't decide to remember. You can only decide to write. That's the whole logic of the pattern in one sentence.

## Rules and exceptions

**Never put a past-tense verb in front of ように when you mean purpose.** Not because it's ungrammatical, but because it quietly turns into something else. {{wasureru|ta|忘[わす]れた}}ように means *as if he'd forgotten* — a comparison, not a goal. So `忘れたように、ノートに書きます` doesn't say what you think it says.

**Politeness lives at the end of the sentence, never before ように.** `読めますように、大きく書きました` is wrong mid-sentence. The clause before ように is always plain; the final verb carries the politeness for the whole thing.

> There is one place where ますように is not only fine but standard: at the very end of a sentence, alone, as a wish. It's a fossil — a leftover shape that survived because people kept saying it. See the casual section below.

The most common wrong guess is putting a **fully controllable action** before ように. Something like `日本語を勉強するように、毎日ノートに書きます` sounds strange, because studying is a thing you simply decide to do — there's no gap for ように to bridge. The fix is usually to reach for the potential form and describe the *state* you want instead: {{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}が{{wakaru||分[わ]かる}}ように. Rule of thumb: if you could stick "I'll just decide to" in front of the verb and it still makes sense, ように is the wrong tool. Japanese has a separate pattern for deliberate-action goals, and you'll meet it later.

> Watch out for ように after a noun plus の. {{neko||猫[ねこ]}}のように{{aruku||歩[ある]く}} means *to walk like a cat* — that's a comparison, a completely different animal that happens to share a spelling. Purpose ように always sits on a verb.

## Casual speech

Here's the good news: ように is one of the rare patterns that doesn't contract, shorten, or shift at all. {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}ように is {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}ように in a boardroom and in a group chat. What changes is only the *end* of the sentence — {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}ように、{{nooto||ノート}}に{{kaku|masu|書[か]きます}} becomes {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}ように、{{nooto||ノート}}に{{kaku||書[か]く}}, and that's the whole difference.

The one form worth memorizing on its own is the standalone wish, which keeps ます even among friends:

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|masu|降[ふ]りません}}ように。
```

*Please, let it not rain tomorrow.*

No main clause, no comma, nothing after it. You'll hear this at shrines, before exams, and muttered at the sky by anyone who left the laundry out.

## Contrast

You already know ば, and it can look deceptively close, because both patterns pair up two events.

```jp
{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{deru-v|stem|出[で]れ}}ば、{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}に{{okureru|masu|遅[おく]れません}}。
```

*If you leave early, you won't be late for the train.*

Compare that with {{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}に{{okureru|nai|遅[おく]れない}}ように、{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{ie||家[いえ]}}を{{deru-v|masu|出[で]ました}} from earlier. ば puts the condition first and the automatic consequence second: leave early → not late, as a general truth. ように flips the emotional order. The goal comes first because the goal came first *in your head*, and the second clause is the choice you made because of it. ば describes how the world works; ように describes why you did something.

The causative せる・{{suru|stem|さ}}せる is worth a second look too, because both patterns are about making things happen.

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}に{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}せました。
```

*I made the child take the medicine.*

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}が{{hitori-de||一人[ひとり]で}}{{nomeru||飲[の]める}}ように、{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{mizu||水[みず]}}に{{ireru-v|masu|入[い]れました}}。
```

*I put the medicine in water so the child could drink it alone.*

The causative applies force to a person: I acted on you, you did the thing. ように applies force to *the situation*: I rearranged the world until the thing became possible, and then it happened on its own. One is a push, the other is clearing the path.

So: goal in front, action behind, plain non-past verb at the seam, and something you can't directly control sitting before ように. That last condition is the one to keep hold of — because when the thing that was impossible finally *does* become possible, Japanese has a pattern built out of this exact よう, and you'll want to see it coming.
caution_notes: The verb before ように must be plain and non-past — politeness belongs only to the final verb of the sentence.
A past-tense verb before ように stops meaning purpose and starts meaning 'as if'.
Put something outside your direct control before ように — a potential form or an intransitive verb — not a fully deliberate action.
Noun + のように is a comparison meaning 'like', not a purpose; purpose ように always attaches to a verb.
