items.explanation_markdown:
You're texting a friend on a slow Saturday afternoon: {{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}か何[なに]か{{miru-v|nai|見[み]ない}}？ — want to watch a movie or something? You don't actually have a title in mind, and you're not going to research one before you hit send. Maybe nothing good is showing, maybe you just want an excuse to hang out and a movie is the easiest thing to name first. か何[なに]か lets you throw out one example — {{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}, a movie — while openly admitting you don't care whether it ends up being that exact thing. Say it plainly, without か何[なに]か, and you've made a specific plan you now have to follow through on. Add か何[なに]か, and you've made an offer that's easy for both of you to bend.

## How it works

か何[なに]か attaches straight onto a noun: **Noun + か何[なに]か**. Nothing conjugates and nothing changes shape — you're not adding a verb ending or picking a form, you're just dropping two small words right after whatever thing you're using as your example.

```jp
{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}か何[なに]か{{miru-v|nai|見[み]ない}}？
```

*Want to watch a movie or something?*

The か here isn't the yes/no question particle you already know from patterns like か{{dou||どう}}か — that か turns a whole clause into "whether." This か is a different, older job: the same か that means "or" when you're choosing between two things (A か B). Pair it with {{nani||何[なに]}}か, "something," and か何[なに]か reads as "or something" tacked straight onto whatever noun came before it. Put the two together right after a noun and you get "[that noun] or something like it" — a real suggestion, wrapped in a shrug. It sounds casual because it basically is casual; you'll hear it constantly among friends and rarely in a formal announcement.

Whatever particle the sentence actually needs — を, が, に, and so on — goes *after* か何[なに]か as a whole unit, not stuck onto the bare noun first. か何[なに]か behaves like the noun grew two extra syllables; the rest of the sentence treats it as one piece.

```jp
{{koohii||コーヒー}}か何[なに]か{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みます}}か。
```

*Would you like coffee or something?*

Here か何[なに]か sits between {{koohii||コーヒー}} and {{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みます}}, doing the job a plain object marker を would otherwise do. Once か何[なに]か is in the sentence, you drop を entirely — a bare noun plus を plus か何[なに]か is not something anyone says, even though you might expect the object marker to still be needed somewhere. か何[なに]か already tells the listener what role {{koohii||コーヒー}} is playing.

You can also put か何[なに]か in front of {{aru||ある}}, when you're asking whether something — anything in a loose category — happens to be around, rather than hunting for one named item.

```jp
{{tsukue||机[つくえ]}}の{{ue||上[うえ]}}に{{kami-paper||紙[かみ]}}か何[なに]か{{aru|masu|あります}}か。
```

*Is there paper or something on the desk?*

Whoever answers isn't expected to produce paper specifically. A notebook, an envelope, the back of a receipt — anything writable would satisfy the question. That's the whole point of naming {{kami-paper||紙[かみ]}} here: it's a stand-in for "a thing like this," not a strict requirement, and a good answer might hand over something that isn't paper at all.

## Rules and exceptions

か何[なに]か only works when the noun in front of it could plausibly be swapped for something similar without breaking the sentence. That's the real test, and it's worth running before you use か何[なに]か on anything. In {{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}か何[なに]か{{miru-v|nai|見[み]ない}}？, swap {{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}} for {{ongaku||音[おん]楽[がく]}} (music) or {{hon||本[ほん]}} (a book) and the invitation still basically works — some easy, low-effort thing to do together. That's what makes {{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}} a legitimate "example, not the point" noun. If swapping the noun would change what you're actually asking for, か何[なに]か is the wrong tool.

> Don't reach for か何[なに]か when you genuinely mean one specific, known thing. `友達か何か` reads like you're unsure whether the person is actually your friend — almost never what you mean. Say {{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}} alone and drop か何[なに]か entirely; vagueness about a fact, rather than about an example, is not what this pattern is for.

か何[なに]か is built for objects, food, and activities — everyday, replaceable items — not for people's identities or specific locations. That's part of why native speakers wince at trying to bolt it onto {{dare||誰[だれ]}} (who) or {{doko||どこ}} (where): naming a vague place or a vague person is a different kind of vagueness than naming a vague *thing*, and か何[なに]か isn't the tool for it. You'll eventually meet other words built for those jobs; for now, keep か何[なに]か parked on ordinary nouns.

It also helps to notice what か何[なに]か is not doing: it isn't hedging because the speaker is unsure of the facts, and it isn't being polite for politeness's sake. It's a deliberate choice to leave a detail open because the detail genuinely doesn't matter yet. That's a small distinction, but it explains why か何[なに]か shows up so often in casual invitations and offers, and so rarely in anything that reads like a report or a form — nobody fills out an application with "book or something" as an answer.

か何[なに]か can also soften a whole request, so it doesn't come across as a demand, even when what you're describing is generous.

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}に{{hon||本[ほん]}}か何[なに]か{{kau-v|te|買[か]って}}{{ageru|stem|あげよう}}。
```

*I'll buy my younger brother a book or something.*

You haven't picked the book yet — you might not even end up buying a book at all, just something in that general spirit, maybe a game or a magazine. That vagueness is doing real work here: it signals you're being generous and easygoing about the choice, not that you're indecisive or don't care about the gift. Naming one concrete noun instead — {{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{kau-v|te|買[か]って}}{{ageru|stem|あげよう}}, no か何[なに]か — sounds like the decision is already final.

## Contrast: か何[なに]か vs {{souiu||そういう}}・{{kouiu||こういう}}

The words {{souiu||そういう}} and {{kouiu||こういう}} mean "that kind of" and "this kind of" — both point at a category the listener can already picture, because it came up in conversation, because they said it, or because it's obvious from context. か何[なに]か is not that. It doesn't lean on anything already shared between speaker and listener; it introduces the category itself, right there in the sentence.

```jp
{{souiu||そういう}}{{hanashi||話[はなし]}}は{{suki||好[す]き}}じゃない。
```

*I don't like that kind of talk.*

{{souiu||そういう}}{{hanashi||話[はなし]}} only works if you and the listener both already know which kind of {{hanashi||話[はなし]}} is meant — something specific was just said or implied a moment ago. か何[なに]か does the opposite job: it introduces a brand-new example that hasn't come up before, and tells the listener up front not to take it too literally.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{amai||甘[あま]い}}ものか何[なに]か{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}たい。
```

*I'm busy, so I want to eat something sweet or whatever.*

Try swapping in {{souiu||そういう}}もの here and the sentence falls apart — there's no "that kind of thing" already on the table for {{souiu||そういう}} to point back to; nobody has mentioned sweets yet. か何[なに]か doesn't need a category the conversation already agreed on; it invents one on the spot, right where it's used, which is exactly why it works so well for first mentions and offhand suggestions.

Put the two side by side and the split is simple: {{souiu||そういう}}・{{kouiu||こういう}} point backward, at something already named; か何[なに]か points forward, at something you're naming for the very first time and don't intend to pin down. Mixing them up doesn't usually produce nonsense — it just produces a sentence that assumes shared context nobody actually has, which is a strange thing to do to a listener who's hearing an idea for the first time.

## Closing thought

か何[なに]か buys you room to suggest something without committing to it — the noun you name is a placeholder, not a decision, and everyone in the conversation understands that instantly.

```jp
{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}で{{ongaku||音[おん]楽[がく]}}か何[なに]か{{kiku-v|stem|聞[き]き}}たい。
```

*I want to listen to music or something in the park.*

Once you're ready to string several loose examples together instead of offering just one, you'll meet とか — "things like this, things like that" — which does for a whole list what か何[なに]か does for a single, disposable guess.
caution_notes: Don't use か何か when you mean one specific, known thing — 友達か何か sounds like you doubt the person even is your friend.
Once か何か is in the sentence, drop the object marker を — a bare noun plus を plus か何か is never said together.
か何か is for replaceable objects, foods, and activities, not for vague people or vague places.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend texts you: {{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}{{nani||何[なに]}}{{suru||する}}？ (What are you doing this weekend?) You haven't actually decided anything yet — maybe a movie, maybe some shopping, maybe you'll just see how you feel Saturday morning. Naming one single plan would be a lie; you don't have one. Naming nothing feels evasive, like you're dodging the question. What you want is a loose, no-commitment answer: a couple of examples that sketch the shape of your weekend without pinning down exactly what happens. That's the job とか does, and once you have it, this kind of half-decided answer stops feeling awkward to give — you're not lying about your plans, you're just being honest that they aren't plans yet.

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}は{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}とか{{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}}とか{{suru|stem|し}}たいです。
```

*I want to do things like watch a movie or go shopping this weekend.*

とか rides along right after a noun and says, in effect, *this, or something like it*. Say it once and you've named one example from a bigger, unnamed set. Say it twice and you've named two, with the same understanding: there might be more you're just not bothering to list. Neither example is "the plan" — they're both stand-ins for a whole category of things you might feel like doing.

## How it works

Structurally, とか is about as simple as N4 grammar gets: Noun + とか, and if you're naming a second example, Noun + とか again. It attaches straight to the noun — no だ, no です, no conjugation to worry about — and then the rest of the sentence carries its own politeness level as normal, completely independent of とか itself. Whatever verb or adjective follows behaves exactly as it would if とか weren't there at all.

There's no fixed ceiling on how many nouns you can chain this way. Three or four, each followed by its own とか, works by the same rule as two — though past two or three, a list starts to feel less like a casual toss-off and more like you're reciting a full itinerary, which undercuts the whole point of reaching for とか in the first place.

```jp
{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}とか{{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}}したいです。
```

*I want to do stuff like watch a movie, maybe go shopping.*

You can drop the second とか once the listener already gets the idea, the way this sentence does — {{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}} just sits there as a plain second item, and nobody blinks. The full doubled shape is the default you reach for, especially the first time you introduce a list, but it isn't mandatory once the pattern is established in the conversation.

> A single noun + とか is already a complete, valid listing on its own — it doesn't need a partner. It just means "this, and other things in the same category," with the rest left comfortably unsaid.

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}は{{terebi||テレビ}}とか{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}}。
```

*This weekend I'll watch stuff like TV, among other things.*

Notice {{terebi||テレビ}}とか never gets a second とか here — there's no second named example, just an implied "and whatever else." That's the hedge doing its job with a single item, and it's a shape learners tend to under-use, reaching for a full two-noun list even when one example plus とか already says everything they mean.

Because とか attaches to a noun rather than a whole sentence, the resulting noun-plus-とか group behaves exactly like any other noun afterward. It can take が as a subject, を as an object, は as a topic — whatever the sentence needs, the same way any plain noun would.

```jp
{{kudamono||果物[くだもの]}}とか{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}とかが{{karada||体[からだ]}}に{{ii||いい}}です。
```

*Things like fruit and vegetables are good for your body.*

{{kudamono||果物[くだもの]}}とか{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}とか as a whole becomes the subject here, then が marks it as usual. The listener understands you don't mean only those two foods — you mean the whole neighborhood of healthy things they stand in for. Try swapping が for を and the same logic carries straight over: {{kudamono||果物[くだもの]}}とか{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}とかを{{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}} would mean eating things in that same loose category, not just those two items on a plate.

## Rules and exceptions

とか is unmistakably casual. It's the register of texting a friend or chatting over lunch, not the register of a report, a job interview, or answering a doctor precisely about what hurts.

> In careful or formal speech, とか's vagueness reads as sloppy rather than friendly. If you actually need to be exact — a doctor asking what symptom you have, a boss asking what's on today's agenda — name the thing plainly and leave とか out entirely.

The other common trap is mixing up とか with か{{nani||何[なに]}}か, which you already know. か{{nani||何[なに]}}か gestures at one item you can't quite name or don't care to specify — "a movie or something." とか, on the other hand, lays out real, concrete examples of a category, even while leaving the exact edges of that category open. The two aren't interchangeable, even though both sound hedgy and both feel casual.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}か{{nani||何[なに]}}か{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ません}}か。
```

*Want to watch a movie or something tomorrow?*

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}とか{{terebi||テレビ}}とか{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ません}}か。
```

*Want to watch stuff like a movie or TV tomorrow?*

The first sentence is one blurry idea — you haven't even decided it's a movie, could be anything. The second hands over two concrete examples standing in for a bigger, unnamed set of options. Same invitation, same politeness level, very different amount of information given to the listener. If someone answers the second question with "どっち？" (which one?), that's a fair response — you handed them two real options to choose between, not one vague placeholder.

One more thing worth knowing: とか is built for nouns, not for handing off someone else's exact words. If you're quoting what a friend said, casually, that's って's job, not とか's — don't reach for とか just because both patterns feel relaxed and conversational. They solve different problems that happen to share the same casual register.

In speech, a noun plus とか can even be the whole answer by itself. Asked {{nani||何[なに]}}が{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}たい？ (What do you feel like eating?), you can just say {{niku||肉[にく]}}とか。(Something like meat, I guess.) and trail off — the noun-plus-とか group already carries a complete thought, so the rest of the sentence is genuinely optional in casual talk, not just shortened.

## Contrast

The word {{souiu||そういう}} points back at "that kind of" thing once a category already exists in the conversation. とか is how you build that category out loud in the first place, by naming a few of its members; {{souiu||そういう}} is how you refer back to the whole category once it's already on the table. One creates, the other recalls.

```jp
{{souiu||そういう}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}が{{suki||好[す]き}}です。
```

*I like that kind of cooking.*

```jp
{{sushi||寿[す]司[し]}}とか{{raamen||ラーメン}}とか、{{souiu||そういう}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}が{{suki||好[す]き}}です。
```

*I like that kind of food — sushi, ramen, things along those lines.*

Name the examples with とか first, then wrap them up with {{souiu||そういう}}, and you've done in one breath what would otherwise take a whole extra sentence: given a couple of concrete anchors, then pointed at the entire category they represent. Learners who skip straight to {{souiu||そういう}} without ever having named anything leave the listener wondering what category they even mean — {{souiu||そういう}} has nothing to point back at yet.

The two patterns also differ in how heavy they feel. とか is light — you can toss out one or two examples mid-sentence without slowing down. {{souiu||そういう}} carries a little more weight; it asks the listener to hold an entire category in mind at once, which is exactly why it works best after とか has already done the work of sketching that category out with real examples.

とか's whole job is staying loose — a couple of named examples standing in for a category you don't feel like spelling out completely. Hold onto that habit of trailing off after a short list; it's exactly the kind of half-settled sentence that ところが, at N3, loves to interrupt, flipping something you thought was decided into something unexpected. For now, the win is smaller and more immediate: you can finally answer {{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}{{nani||何[なに]}}{{suru||する}}？ honestly, without pretending you've already decided.
caution_notes: とか is casual — swap it out (or drop it) in formal writing and careful speech, since its vagueness reads as sloppy rather than friendly there.
A single noun plus とか already implies "and other things like it" — you don't need a second とか to make that reading valid, even though pairing two examples is the more common shape.
Don't confuse とか with か何か: とか lists real, specific examples of a category, while か何か gestures at one item you can't or won't name.
とか attaches to nouns for listing, not to someone else's exact words — reach for って when you're casually quoting what somebody said.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture your older brother waking up with a fever. He should stay in bed today — that's the obvious move. Instead he gets dressed and walks out the door to work like nothing happened. English has a whole family of words for that shrug — still, anyway, regardless — but Japanese has one word built for exactly this move: それでも.

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{netsu||熱[ねつ]}}が{{aru|ta|あった}}。それでも{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}。
```

*My older brother had a fever. Even so, he went to work.*

That's the whole shape of it. State what happened. Put a period down. Drop それでも in as its own little sentence-opener. State what happened next — something the first sentence should have stopped, and didn't.

That gap between what should happen and what actually does is the whole point of the word. それでも doesn't soften the obstacle, apologize for it, or explain it away — it just names the obstacle, closes the sentence on it, and lets the next sentence walk straight through it anyway.

## How it works

それでも always sits between two separate ideas: **Sentence. + それでも + Sentence.** The first sentence lays out a fact that creates resistance — bad weather, an injury, a lack of sleep, anything that would normally get in the way of what comes next. The second sentence reports that the resistance didn't work.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}{{iru-exist|ta|いた}}。それでも{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{sanpo-suru|ta|散[さん]歩[ぽ]した}}。
```

*It was raining. Even so, my brother went for a walk.*

Notice that それでも doesn't attach to anything — it isn't glued onto a verb stem the way a conjugated ending would be, so there's nothing here to conjugate. Past tense, present tense, casual or polite, it stays それでも no matter what came before it. Its only job is standing at the front of the second sentence and pointing back at the first one.

That's also why it never changes shape for politeness. The sentences around it might be polite or plain, but それでも itself is neither — it's just a connector, not a verb or an adjective, so there's no です or ます form of it to reach for.

It also doesn't shrink in casual speech the way some polite words do — わからない becoming わかんない, or では becoming じゃ. それでも already sounds plain and complete on its own, so there's nothing left to trim, and you'll hear it exactly this way whether the conversation is formal or between old friends.

You'll also see it show up mid-sentence, right after a clause joined with が, instead of after a fresh period. It's still doing the same job — the が just means the writer chose to keep both halves in one breath instead of splitting them into two sentences.

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}が、それでも{{netsu||熱[ねつ]}}は{{sagaru|nai|下[さ]がらなかった}}。
```

*My brother took his medicine, but even then his fever didn't go down.*

Either way — full stop or が — the test is the same: can you point at the sentence right before それでも and name the thing it should have blocked? If yes, you're using it correctly.

Both versions show up constantly in ordinary storytelling — someone recapping their weekend, a coworker explaining why they're late, a doctor summarizing a patient's stubborn symptoms. Anywhere someone reports "this happened, and then, against expectation, this also happened," それでも is doing quiet work in the background.

## Rules and exceptions

それでも needs the first sentence to carry real weight. It has to describe an obstacle a listener would nod along to — "yes, that should have been a problem." Drop in something trivial and それでも starts to sound like you're announcing a fight that never happened.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}は{{setsumei||説[せつ]明[めい]}}を三[さん]回[かい]{{suru|ta|した}}。それでも{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{imi||意[い]味[み]}}が{{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からなかった}}。
```

*The teacher explained it three times. Even so, I didn't understand the meaning.*

Three explanations is genuine effort — the kind of thing that should have produced understanding. それでも earns its keep here because the outcome really does fight against the setup.

Compare that to a setup with barely any weight — one quick reminder, say, instead of three full explanations. それでも would feel like overkill there, as if you were bracing the listener for a much bigger fight than the sentence actually describes. The word carries its own sense of scale, so save it for obstacles that are genuinely heavy.

> それでも always looks backward at something already stated. It can't reach forward into a hypothetical — a sentence like "if the exam turns out to be hard, I'll study anyway" isn't a job for それでも. It wants a sentence that already happened or is already true, not a guess about a future that hasn't landed yet.

The obstacle also doesn't have to be one blunt fact — a whole earlier situation can serve as the setup, as long as a reader can point back and name what it was.

```jp
{{setsumei||説[せつ]明[めい]}}は{{muzukashii|ta|難[むずか]しかった}}。それでも{{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}}は{{ganbatte||頑張[がんば]って}}{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}した。
```

*The explanation was difficult. Even so, the student kept at their studying.*

This is also why それでも rarely opens a conversation cold. Someone hearing it for the first time needs the earlier sentence to be sitting right there — spoken out loud a moment ago, or written just above. Start a chat with それでも and nobody knows what "even so" is supposed to be answering.

## Contrast

Here's a piece of trivia that makes それでも easier to hold onto: it's literally {{sore||それ}} (that) plus {{demo||でも}} (even) — "even that" worn down into "even so." Which means you already knew half of this word. {{demo||でも}} on its own means but/however, and それでも just points that {{demo||でも}} squarely at the sentence sitting right in front of it.

Swap それでも for a bare {{demo||でも}} and you lose that pointing-back feeling. {{demo||でも}} can open a sentence out of nowhere, contrasting two things that were never really in tension to begin with.

```jp
{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}は{{warui|ta|悪[わる]かった}}。{{demo||でも}}、{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}は{{kirei||きれい}}だった。
{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}は{{warui|ta|悪[わる]かった}}。それでも{{watashitachi||私[わたし]たち}}は{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}を{{aruku|ta|歩[ある]いた}}。
```

*The weather was bad. But the park was pretty.*
*The weather was bad. Even so, we walked through the park.*

The first pair is just two facts sitting side by side — bad weather, pretty park, no real friction between them. The second pair says the bad weather should have kept everyone indoors, and it didn't; that resistance is the part only それでも carries.

That's the whole pattern: name the obstacle, then let それでも announce that it lost. It's a small word to carry that much weight — one clause of setup, one word of pivot, one clause of payoff — but that's exactly why it reads as calm instead of dramatic. It isn't fighting the obstacle; it's just reporting, flatly, that the obstacle didn't get its way.

Hold onto the {{demo||でも}} comparison — once {{soko||そこ}}で shows up, you'll see it pick up right where それでも leaves off, moving the story from "and yet, nothing changed" to "so here's what I did about it."
caution_notes: それでも always needs a real, already-stated obstacle in the sentence before it — used on something trivial, it can sound like you're overreacting.
それでも can't point at a hypothetical; the sentence before it has to describe something that already happened or is already true, not a future guess.
それでも rarely opens a conversation on its own — without an earlier sentence naming the obstacle, listeners won't know what it's answering.

items.explanation_markdown:
You left the house and the sky opened up on you halfway to the station. You didn't just stand there getting soaked — you did something about it. In Japanese, the sentence that reports what you decided to do next often opens with そこで, a word that works like "so, at that point" — it's the hinge between a situation you found yourself in and the deliberate move you made in response.

そこで doesn't just mean "and then." It carries a small implication: something happened, you registered it, and you acted. That makes it different from a plain time-sequence word like {{soshite||そして}} (and then) — {{soshite||そして}} just lines events up in order, while そこで insists that the second event happened *because of* the first one, as a response someone chose to make. Keep that piece in mind; it's the whole engine of the pattern.

## How そこで works

The shape is simple: one full sentence describing a situation, a period, then そこで, a comma, and a second full sentence describing the action taken because of that situation. そこで always opens the second sentence — it never sits in the middle of one sentence joined by a comma the way から can. You're always looking at two separate sentences, and そこで is the word standing at the start line of the second one, pointing back at the first.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|ta|降[ふ]った}}。
そこで、{{chikaku||近[ちか]く}}の{{kissaten||喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[てん]}}に{{hairu-v|ta|入[はい]った}}。
```
*It rained.*
*So I went into a nearby coffee shop.*

The first sentence just reports what happened — no judgment, no plan yet. The second sentence is where the story turns: you noticed the rain, and そこで marks the exact point where noticing became doing. Drop そこで and the two sentences just sit next to each other with no signal that one caused the other; the connection has to be guessed from context instead of stated.

```jp
{{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}の{{imi||意[い]味[み]}}が{{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からなかった}}。
そこで、{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{kiku-v|ta|聞[き]いた}}。
```
*I didn't understand what the homework meant.*
*So I asked the teacher.*

Here's the part that matters most about そこで, and it's the one rule everything else in this lesson hangs off of: the second sentence has to be an action — something the speaker actively did — not another fact or feeling. `宿題の意味が分からなかった。そこで、少し不安だった。` (I didn't understand the homework. So I felt a little anxious.) technically parses as a sentence, but it reads strangely, because feeling anxious isn't a response you chose the way asking a question is. A feeling just happens to you; そこで wants something you *did*. Keep the sentence after そこで doing something, not just being something, and the pattern will always sound natural.

That constraint is also what tells you そこで apart from a simple list of events. If you can't answer "what did the speaker decide to do about it?" with the second sentence, そこで is probably the wrong connector for that pair.

そこで can also chain forward. Once a second sentence has been set up with そこで, the story is free to keep going in plain past tense — {{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}の{{imi||意[い]味[み]}}が{{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からなかった}}。そこで、{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{kiku-v|ta|聞[き]いた}}。{{wakaru|ta|分[わ]かった}}。 (I didn't understand the homework. So I asked the teacher. I understood.) — without needing another そこで to hold the third sentence in place. The connector only has to fire once, at the pivot from situation to response; everything after that just continues the story in order.

## Rules and exceptions

そこで is a narration word. It shows up naturally when you're explaining a sequence of events — telling a story, writing a report, walking someone through what happened after the fact — and it sounds a little formal or writerly for quick back-and-forth chat. If a friend asks "why did you do that?" a plain {{dakara||だから}} answer fits the moment better than reaching for そこで, which reads more like the voice of someone recounting the whole episode from a bit of distance.

```jp
{{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|ta|痛[いた]かった}}。
そこで、{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}。
```
*My head hurt.*
*So I took some medicine.*

That sentence works equally well spoken or written, but notice the shape: a state ({{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|ta|痛[いた]かった}}) followed by a clear, chosen action ({{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}). Swap the order — put the action first and the state second — and そこで stops making sense, because by definition it's always pointing backward at whatever came right before it.

This is also why そこで never attaches directly to a noun or an adjective the way か{{nani||何[なに]}}か or とか do. It only ever opens a full sentence, because its whole job is to summarize "given the situation just described" in one word before handing off to the response. There's no shorter form and no version that tucks into the middle of a clause.

> そこで is spelled and pronounced exactly like {{soko||そこ}} (there) plus the particle で (at / by means of). When {{soko||そこ}} is pointing back at a place already mentioned, and で is just marking where something happens, you get the same two syllables meaning something completely different.

```jp
{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}。
そこで、{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}を{{matsu|te|待[ま]って}}{{iru-exist|ta|いた}}。
```
*I went to the park.*
*There, I waited for my friend.*

Read that second sentence out loud and it looks identical to the connector. The difference is entirely about what came before it: {{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}} (park) was just introduced, so {{soko||そこ}} has something concrete to point at, and で is simply saying where the waiting happened. If the previous sentence names no place at all, there's nothing for {{soko||そこ}} to refer to, and the reading collapses back into the connector — there's no situation-and-response pair to explain otherwise. When you're unsure which reading you're looking at, ask whether a place was just named in the sentence before it; if yes, check the locative reading first, because that's the one a bare grammar gloss won't warn you about.

## Contrast: そこで vs {{sorede||それで}}も

You already know {{sorede||それで}}も, and it shares そこで's job of opening a sentence that responds to the one before it — but it pulls in the opposite direction. そこで says the second sentence follows naturally from the first: situation, then response, the kind of link you'd expect. {{sorede||それで}}も says the second sentence happened in spite of the first.

```jp
{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}。
{{sorede||それで}}も、{{netsu||熱[ねつ]}}は{{sagaru|nai|下[さ]がらなかった}}。
```
*I took the medicine.*
*Even so, my fever didn't go down.*

Swap {{sorede||それで}}も for そこで in that pair and the sentence stops making sense — a fever that won't go down isn't something anyone decides to do in response to medicine; there's no decision being reported, just an obstacle that held. {{sorede||それで}}も points back at the whole situation: "even given everything I just told you, this still happened." It never announces a chosen action the way そこで does, and that's the fastest way to tell the two apart once you've got a candidate sentence in front of you.

So the quick test: if the second sentence is something the speaker decided to do because of the first, reach for そこで. If it's something that happened anyway, against what you'd expect, {{sorede||それで}}も is doing the work instead. Once you've asked "is this a decision or a push-through?", the right connector usually picks itself.

It helps to line the two up side by side in your head. そこで: situation, then chosen response — smooth, expected. {{sorede||それで}}も: situation, then persistence in spite of it — the situation doesn't get resolved, it just gets pushed through. Both open a new sentence and both look backward, but only one of them is ever reporting a decision.

Hold onto that shape — you'll meet a close cousin soon, {{sono||その}}ため, which points even more directly at the reason behind the second sentence rather than the moment of deciding to act on it.
caution_notes: そこで looks and sounds exactly like そこ (there) plus the particle で, so check whether the previous sentence just named a place before reading it as the connector.
The sentence after そこで needs to be a real action the speaker chose to take, not just another fact or feeling — pairing it with a state instead of a decision reads oddly.
そこで belongs to narration and explanation, so it can sound stiff as a quick spoken answer to a casual "why did you do that?"
items.mnemonic_text: When the school robot freezes mid-bow before the show, Sei cracks her knuckles and says "<reading>So, code!</reading>": <grammar>so, faced with that, she acts</grammar>. <reading>そこで</reading>、{{watashi||私}}は{{sore||それ}}を{{naosu|ta|直した}}。

items.explanation_markdown:
Your train stalls on the tracks for twenty minutes, and by the time you reach the office, everyone is already sitting down for the meeting. When a coworker asks what happened, you don't need to retell the whole story of the delay — you can report it like a headline: cause, then effect, one sentence pointing straight at the next.

```jp
{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{okureru|ta|遅[おく]れた}}。
そのため、{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}に{{chikoku-suru|ta|遅[ち]刻[こく]した}}。
```
*The train was delayed.*
*Because of that, I was late to the meeting.*

そのため sits at the start of the second sentence and points straight back at the one before it — that first sentence is the cause, and everything after そのため is simply what came of it. It's already a fused word, built from {{sono||その}} (that) plus a piece meaning "for the sake of," so it never splits apart, conjugates, or changes shape no matter what surrounds it.

Notice, too, what そのため is quietly leaving out. It never says whether the delay was expected, whether you're annoyed about it, or whether being late was a big deal — it just states the link between the two facts and moves on. That flatness is the whole point: it's a connector for reporting outcomes, not for narrating feelings about them.

## How it works

そのため always follows a full, complete sentence — plain or polite, past or present — and opens the next one, usually with a comma right after it. You're not attaching it to a verb stem or a noun the way most particles work; it just sits there on its own, functioning as what you could call a **consequence connector** — a little word whose only job is to link "this happened" to "and because of it, so did this." There's no verb form to memorize and no particle to swap in or out. All of its work is done by where it sits, not by how it bends.

Because そのため needs a complete, finished sentence in front of it, you'll never see it wedged directly onto a noun the way か{{nani||何[なに]}}か or とか attach to one. The cause has to close itself off as its own full thought first, period and all, before そのため can point back at it.

- Always follows a full sentence, never a bare noun or verb stem.
- Keeps exactly the same shape whether the sentences around it are casual or polite.
- States a plain, factual consequence — not something anyone decided to do.
- Needs the cause already spoken or written — it never opens a new topic out of nowhere.

```jp
{{kaze-cold||風邪[かぜ]}}をひいた。
そのため、{{gakkou-v||学[がっ]校[こう]}}を{{yasumu|ta|休[やす]んだ}}。
```
*I caught a cold.*
*Because of that, I stayed home from school.*

The politeness of the surrounding sentences never touches そのため itself. Watch what happens when the whole exchange gets dressed up:

```jp
{{saifu||財[さい]布[ふ]}}をなくしました。
そのため、{{okane||お金[かね]}}が{{aru|masu|ありませんでした}}。
```
*I lost my wallet.*
*Because of that, I didn't have any money.*

Compare that to the cold example above — same connector, same job, even though one conversation is casual and the other is polite. そのため doesn't conjugate, doesn't take a particle of its own, and doesn't care what tense or politeness level the sentences around it are in. It's the one constant in an otherwise shifting sentence.

## Rules and exceptions

そのため needs a real sentence stating a cause sitting right in front of it. You can't open cold with そのため and expect the listener to guess what "that" refers to — the cause has to already be on the table, whether it's the sentence directly before or something explained a little earlier in the same conversation. It also carries a slightly formal register — a way of describing how casual or dressed-up something sounds — so you'll run into it constantly in news reports, workplace emails, and explanations, more than in relaxed chat about your weekend.

> Watch out for `そのために` — same characters, one extra に, a completely different job. That version means "in order to" or "for the sake of that," pointing forward at a goal you're working toward, not backward at a cause you're reporting. そのため looks back at what already happened; そのために looks forward at what you're trying to make happen.

There's no casual, shrunk-down version of そのため the way です contracts to じゃ in speech. It's already about as plain and portable as a connector gets, so you'll meet it in nearly the same shape everywhere you read or hear it — spoken news, a coworker's email, or a friend explaining why they're late, though a friend is just as likely to reach for something looser instead.

You'll also hear そのため used out loud, not just on the page. A speaker giving a status update in a meeting, or a train announcement explaining a delay, both lean on it — it's the sound of someone laying out a cause and then telling you plainly what followed, without dressing the second sentence up as their own opinion or reaction. That's part of why it feels a step more formal than something like {{dakara||だから}}: it's built for reporting, not for reacting.

## Contrast: そのため vs {{soko||そこ}}で vs {{dakara||だから}}

You already have {{soko||そこ}}で for "so, in response to that" — but the two pull in different directions. {{soko||そこ}}で frames what comes next as something a person decided to do about the situation. そのため frames it as a plain consequence, whether or not anyone decided anything at all.

```jp
{{soko||そこ}}で、{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}を{{kau-v|ta|買[か]った}}。
そのため、{{fuku||服[ふく]}}が{{nureru|ta|濡[ぬ]れた}}。
```
*So I went and bought an umbrella.*
*Because of that, my clothes got wet.*

Same rainy afternoon, told two ways. Buying the umbrella is a choice made **in response** to the rain — that's {{soko||そこ}}で's territory. Getting rained on before reaching the store isn't a choice at all, just a plain result, and that's exactly what そのため reports.

There's a third connector worth placing next to these two: {{dakara||だから}}, the casual "so" you already reach for with friends. Picture someone who wasn't feeling well and just went to bed early.

```jp
{{dakara||だから}}、{{yasumu|ta|休[やす]んだ}}。
そのため、{{yasumu|ta|休[やす]んだ}}。
```
*So I rested.*
*Because of that, I rested.*

Both sentences describe the exact same choice, but they'd land in different rooms. {{dakara||だから}} is what you'd actually say out loud to a friend — quick, casual, unremarkable. そのため is what you'd write in a note explaining an absence, or what a narrator might say summing up a scene — a little more distant, a little more report-like. Swapping one for the other doesn't change the facts, only how formal the retelling sounds. Picture a text to a friend using {{dakara||だから}}, and a message to a teacher explaining the same absence using そのため — same event, two different rooms.

If a sentence describes someone actively doing something about a situation, {{soko||そこ}}で usually reads more naturally. If it describes what simply resulted — good news or bad, chosen or not — and you want that neutral, slightly written tone, reach for そのため instead of forcing an active-sounding connector onto a passive fact.

The shape you just practiced — a full sentence, そのため, another full sentence — comes back almost immediately with {{suru||する}}と, which uses the same two-sentence structure to walk through what happened next in a sequence rather than what one sentence caused. For now, keep そのため on hand for the plain, factual "and because of that" link, and let {{dakara||だから}} and {{soko||そこ}}で carry the sentences where someone is actually speaking casually or choosing what to do next.
caution_notes: そのため only works when the sentence right before it (or clearly established just before) states a cause — don't open with it out of nowhere.
そのため itself never conjugates or changes with politeness level; only the sentences around it do.
Don't confuse そのため with the look-alike そのために, which points forward at a goal instead of back at a cause.
そのため reads as a neutral, almost report-style connector; for a livelier, more casual retelling, だから or そこで usually fits better.

items.explanation_markdown:
You open the window to let some air in, and the second your hand touches the frame you notice it — rain, coming down steady, and you had no idea it had even started. In Japanese, the connector that carries you from the first action straight into the surprise that followed it is すると.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{akeru|ta|開[あ]けた}}。すると{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}{{iru-exist|ta|いた}}。
```

*I opened the window. Then it was raining.*

すると sits at the very front of the second sentence, right after a full stop. It never changes shape — no conjugation, no politeness form, nothing to memorize beyond the word itself. That's the whole mechanic: one complete sentence, a period, すると, another complete sentence. The first sentence is the trigger — something you did, or something that was simply true — and the すると sentence reports what showed up right afterward, almost like you're narrating a scene as it unfolds in front of you.

## How it works

The first sentence can be in plain past tense, describing a single thing that actually happened once. That's the most common shape you'll meet: you did something, and すると hands you straight into what you found.

```jp
{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{kaeru-v|ta|帰[かえ]った}}。すると{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{tsukue||机[つくえ]}}の{{ue||上[うえ]}}で{{neru|te|寝[ね]て}}{{iru-exist|ta|いた}}。
```

*I went home. Then the cat was sleeping on the desk.*

```jp
{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}の{{namae||名[な]前[まえ]}}を{{yobu|ta|呼[よ]んだ}}。すると{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{okiru|ta|起[お]きた}}。
```

*I called the cat's name. Then the cat woke up.*

Notice who's doing what in each half. You call the cat's name — that's your action. The cat waking up is not your action; it's what happened as a direct, practically automatic consequence of yours. That's the feel すると carries: the second half is something you observed or discovered, not something you decided to do.

There's a second use of the same word, and it's easy to miss the first time you meet it. If the first sentence is in plain non-past form instead of past, すると describes a pattern that holds every time, not a one-off event.

```jp
{{maiasa||毎[まい]朝[あさ]}}、{{denki||電[でん]気[き]}}を{{tsukeru||つける}}。すると{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{okiru||起[お]きる}}。
```

*Every morning I turn on the light. Then the cat wakes up.*

Same connector, same two-sentence shape — the only thing that shifted is the tense of the first half, from {{tsukeru|ta|つけた}} (turned on, once) to {{tsukeru||つける}} (turn on, every time). That tense shift is what tells the listener whether you're recounting a specific morning or describing a routine.

## Rules and exceptions

The part that trips people up is what すると is *not* allowed to introduce. The second sentence has to be something that happens on its own — a fact, a discovery, someone or something else's reaction. It cannot be your own decision about what to do next.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}を{{yobu|ta|呼[よ]んだ}}。すると{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}が{{kuru-v|ta|来[き]た}}。
```

*I called my friend. Then my friend came.*

That works because "my friend came" is their action, reported as a consequence — not a plan you're announcing. Compare that to something like `友達を呼んだ。すると友達と話しましょう。` — trying to use すると to lead into your own proposal ("let's talk") is wrong. The moment the second half is a request, an invitation, an order, or a statement of intent, すると can't carry it; that job belongs to a different connector entirely.

> すると almost always reports something that has already happened or that reliably happens — treat it as a narrator's word, not a planner's word. If you catch yourself about to write a volitional form (〜ましょう, 〜よう) or a request after すると, stop and pick another connector.

The other trap is reaching for すると when the second sentence actually contradicts what you'd expect from the first. すると is neutral — mildly surprising at most, never a reversal. A genuine reversal needs a different word, which is exactly what the contrast section below is for.

## Contrast

You've already met {{soko||そこ}}で, for when the second sentence is a deliberate response you chose to make, and {{sorede||それで}}も, for when the second sentence happens in spite of what the first one set up. Line all three up against the same scene and the differences become obvious.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}を{{yobu|ta|呼[よ]んだ}}。{{soko||そこ}}で{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}と{{hanasu-v|ta|話[はな]した}}。
```

*I called my friend. So I talked with my friend.*

Here the second half is something you decided to do next, on purpose — that's {{soko||そこ}}で's territory. Swap in すると and it reads as though the talking just happened to you, which isn't the sense you want when you're describing your own choice.

```jp
何[なん]度[ど]も{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}を{{yobu|ta|呼[よ]んだ}}。{{sorede||それで}}も{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}は{{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]なかった}}。
```

*I called my friend again and again. Even so, my friend didn't come.*

Here the second half pushes against the first — you kept calling, and yet nothing came of it. That gap between effort and result is what {{sorede||それで}}も is built for, and it's exactly the gap すると refuses to carry. すると's version of this scene simply has the friend showing up, no surprise, no letdown — the plainest possible next beat in the story.

So the three sit in a row: すると narrates the next thing that happened, {{soko||そこ}}で narrates the next thing you chose to do, {{sorede||それで}}も narrates the thing that happened in spite of what came before.

Worth holding onto for later: {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}}に flips a situation the opposite way rather than simply continuing it forward, which is a slightly different move than any of these three — more on that at N3.

For now, the shape to remember is small: one finished sentence, すると, one more sentence reporting what followed. Read a few lines of any story written in Japanese and you'll start noticing it everywhere — it's one of the plainest ways native writers move a scene forward one beat at a time.
caution_notes: すると cannot introduce your own deliberate next move — use そこで when the second half is a choice you made rather than something you noticed happen.
Never follow すると with a request, invitation, or volitional form (〜ましょう, 〜よう); it only narrates what happened or what reliably happens, never what you intend to do.
If the second sentence happens in spite of what the first one set up, that's それでも's job, not すると's.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture texting a friend about Saturday's get-together: "Is everyone coming?" Almost everyone — one person can't make it. You want to say "everyone except Ken," and Japanese has a clean, single word for that job: 以[い]外[がい] (igai), meaning "except" or "other than." It attaches directly onto whichever noun you're pulling out of the group, so you never have to build a whole clause around it.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{minna||みんな}}{{kuru-v|masu|来[き]ます}}。
```
*Everyone except me is coming.*

Notice what happened there: 以[い]外[がい] sits right after {{watashi||私[わたし]}} (me) — no verb, no connector, just a person and then the word that says "not counting this one." That's the entire shape of the pattern: **Noun + 以[い]外[がい]**.

## How it works

以[い]外[がい] always follows a noun — whatever you're carving out of a larger group. Once it's attached, everything else in the sentence is understood to apply to the rest of that group, not to the noun sitting in front of 以[い]外[がい].

If what you want to exclude is an action rather than a thing, you can't hand 以[い]外[がい] a bare verb — it needs a noun first, so you build one with こと (a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a thing you can talk about):

```jp
{{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}} → {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}}こと
```
*to swim → swimming (the thing itself)*

```jp
{{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}}こと以[い]外[がい]、{{supootsu||スポーツ}}が{{nigate||苦[にが]手[て]}}です。
```
*Other than swimming, I'm bad at sports.*

Two shapes show up constantly, and they're really just 以[い]外[がい] riding on a particle you already know:

- **以[い]外[がい]に** — leans toward "besides / in addition to." Common with a positive verb ("besides X, also Y") and just as common with a negative one ("nothing besides X").
- **以[い]外[がい]は** — leans toward "as for everything except X," setting X up as the one exception to whatever comes next.

```jp
{{ongaku||音[おん]楽[がく]}}以[い]外[がい]に{{shumi||趣[しゅ]味[み]}}が{{aru|masu|ありません}}。
```
*I don't have a hobby besides music.*

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}以[い]外[がい]に{{eigo||英[えい]語[ご]}}も{{hanaseru|masu|話[はな]せます}}。
```
*Besides Japanese, I can also speak English.*

```jp
{{doyoubi||土[ど]曜[よう]日[び]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*I study every day except Saturday.*

に and は aren't doing anything new here — they're the same particles you've used since week one. に leans toward "additionally," は leans toward "as for the rest of the group." Neither one changes what 以[い]外[がい] itself means; they just tint the sentence around it.

## Rules and exceptions

The one rule that trips people up: 以[い]外[がい] wants a noun immediately in front of it. In English, "except" can follow almost any kind of phrase, but Japanese draws a harder line. A bare plain-form verb can't feed straight into 以[い]外[がい].

> Don't write `泳ぐ以外` on its own to mean "other than swimming." A verb needs to be turned into a noun first — usually with こと — before 以[い]外[がい] can attach: {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}}こと以[い]外[がい].

以[い]外[がい] pairs naturally with a negative predicate to mean "only this one." That's not really a separate rule — it's just what "not X except Y" collapses to once you say it out loud:

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{dare-mo||誰[だれ]も}}{{shiru|masu|知[し]りません}}。
```
*No one knows except him.*

Read literally, that's "as for other than him, nobody knows" — which lands as "only he knows." Once you notice that shape, 以[い]外[がい] plus a negative keeps showing up wherever the real meaning is "only."

> 以[い]外[がい] marks what's outside the group — it says nothing about how big the group itself is.

```jp
{{sakana||魚[さかな]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{suki||好[す]き}}です。
```
*I like everything except fish.*

That sentence tells you fish is out. It doesn't tell you whether "everything" means two dishes or twenty — 以[い]外[がい] draws the boundary, not the headcount.

以[い]外[がい] doesn't care about politeness level either. It sits comfortably in plain speech and in です・ます sentences without changing shape, so you don't need a separate casual version to learn — the word itself never bends. In a quick spoken answer, people will sometimes drop the は or に and let bare 以[い]外[がい] carry the whole thought as a fragment — someone asks what you don't eat, and {{sakana||魚[さかな]}}以[い]外[がい]。 is a complete answer on its own.

## Contrast

Everything else you've learned so far — {{sorede||それで}}も, {{soko||そこ}}で, {{sono||その}}ため, {{suru||する}}と — links two full sentences together. 以[い]外[がい] works differently: it's a small word riding directly on a noun, not a bridge between clauses. You can't swap it in for one of those connectors and expect the sentence to hold together; they're built for different jobs.

Where they do overlap is in mood, and {{sorede||それで}}も is the closest one to check yourself against. {{sorede||それで}}も says "even given that, X still happened" — it concedes something and pushes past it:

```jp
{{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|ta|痛[いた]かった}}。
{{sorede||それで}}も{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}。
```
*I had a headache.*
*Even so, I went to work.*

以[い]外[がい] doesn't concede anything; it just draws a line around one item and says "not this one." If you ever reach for {{sorede||それで}}も to mean "except for this," that's the moment to reach for 以[い]外[がい] instead — {{sorede||それで}}も answers "what happened anyway?" while 以[い]外[がい] answers "what's left out?"

以[い]外[がい] also isn't the same word as {{hoka||他[ほか]}} (ほか), even though both get translated as "other." {{hoka||他[ほか]}} is a plain noun — "another one" — that can stand on its own and take its own particles, like a subject or an object. 以[い]外[がい] never stands alone; it only exists attached to the noun it's excluding.

This is worth holding onto beyond today: 以[い]外[がい] belongs to a small family of patterns that bolt straight onto a noun instead of linking two sentences. You'll meet another member of that family at N3 in 以[い]来[らい], which uses the same "Noun +" shape to mean "ever since."
caution_notes: 以外 needs a noun right in front of it — a bare plain-form verb has to become a noun with こと first, as in 泳ぐこと以外.
以外 only marks what's left out of the group; it says nothing about how large the rest of the group is.
以外 plus a negative predicate usually means 'only this one,' not a double exclusion, so read 彼以外は誰も知りません as 'only he knows.'
